                                                                                  CORE4 ENGINEERS LIMITED
Our Company was originally formed as a partnership firm under the name and style “Core4 Engineers” in Mysore, Karnataka, under the provisions of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, pursuant to a partnership deed
dated June 06, 2014, as amended from time to time and was registered with the Registrar of Firms, Mysore, on July 11, 2014. Subsequently, the partnership firm was converted into a private limited company “Core4
Engineers Private Limited” on February 03, 2022 pursuant to the provisions of Chapter XXI of the Companies Act, 2013 and fresh a Certificate of Incorporation dated February 03, 2022 was issued by the Registrar of
Companies, Central Registration Centre. Thereafter, our company was converted from a private limited company to a public limited company, pursuant to a special resolution passed in the extraordinary general meeting
of our shareholders held on February 27, 2025 and the name of our Company was changed to “Core4 Engineers Limited” with a fresh certificate of incorporation dated April 23, 2025, issued to our Company by the
Assistant Registrar of Companies/Deputy Registrar of Companies/ Registrar of Companies, Central Processing Centre. For further details on incorporation and registered office of our Company, see “History and Certain
Corporate Matters” on page 255.

  NEWSPAPER), AND ALL EDITIONS OF THE KANNADA DAILY NEWSPAPER, [●] (KANNADA BEING THE REGIONAL LANGUAGE OF KARNATAKA, WHERE OUR
  REGISTERED OFFICE IS LOCATED), AT LEAST TWO WORKING DAYS PRIOR TO THE BID / ISSUE OPENING DATE AND SHALL BE MADE AVAILABLE TO BSE
  LIMITED FOR UPLOADING ON THEIR WEBSITE IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE SEBI ICDR REGULATIONS.
  In case of any revision in the Price Band, the Bid / Issue Period will be extended by at least three additional Working Days after such revision in the Price Band, subject to the Bid / Issue Period not
  exceeding 10 Working Days. In cases of force majeure, banking strike or similar unforeseen circumstances, our Company may, in consultation with the BRLM, for reasons to be recorded in writing,
  extend the Bid / Issue Period for a minimum period of one Working Day, subject to the Bid / Issue Period not exceeding 10 Working Days. Any revision in the Price band and the revised Bid / Issue
  Period, if applicable, shall be widely disseminated by notification to the Stock Exchange, by issuing a public notice and also by indicating the change on the website of the BRLM and at the terminals
  of the Syndicate Members and by intimation to Designated Intermediaries and the Sponsor Bank, as applicable.
  This Issue is being made through the Book Building process, in terms of Rule 19(2)(b)(i) of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Rules, 1957, as amended (“SCRR”) read with Regulation 252 of the
  SEBI ICDR Regulations and in compliance with Regulation 253(1) and Regulation 253(2) of the SEBI ICDR Regulations wherein not more than 50% of the Net Issue shall be available for allocation
  on a proportionate basis to Qualified Institutional Buyers (“QIBs”, the “QIB Portion”), provided that our Company in consultation with the BRLM, may allocate up to 60% of the QIB Portion to
  Anchor Investors and the basis of such allocation will be on a discretionary basis by our Company in consultation with the BRLM, in accordance with the SEBI ICDR Regulations (the “Anchor
  Investor Portion”), of which, 40% shall be reserved in the following manner: (i) 33.33% shall be available for allocation to domestic Mutual Funds, and (ii) 6.67% shall be available for Life Insurance
  Companies and Pension Funds, subject to valid Bids being received from domestic Mutual Funds, Life Insurance Companies and Pension Funds at or above the Anchor Investor Allocation Price. In
  the event of under-subscription in (ii) above, the allocation may be made to domestic Mutual Funds. In the event of under-subscription, or non-allocation in the Anchor Investor Portion, the balance
  Equity Shares shall be added to the QIB Portion (other than Anchor Investor Portion) (“Net QIB Portion”). Further, 5% of the Net QIB Portion shall be available for allocation on a proportionate
  basis only to Mutual Funds, subject to valid Bids being received at or above the Issue Price, and the remainder of the Net QIB Portion shall be available for allocation on a proportionate basis to all
  QIBs (other than Anchor Investors), including Mutual Funds, subject to valid Bids being received at or above the Issue Price. Further, not less than 15% of the Net Issue shall be available for allocation
  to Non-Institutional Bidders (“Non-Institutional Portion”) on a proportionate basis to Non-Institutional Bidders out of which (a) one third of the portion available to non-institutional bidders shall
  be reserved for applicants with application size of more than two lots and up to such lots equivalent to not more than ₹10.00 lakhs; (b) two third of the portion available to non-institutional bidders
  shall be reserved for applicants with application size of more than ₹10.00 lakhs provided that the unsubscribed portion in either of such sub-categories may be allocated to applicants in the other sub-
  category of Non-Institutional Bidders. Further, not less than 35% of the Net Issue shall be available for allocation to Individual Bidders in accordance with the SEBI ICDR Regulations, subject to
  valid Bids being received from them at or above the Issue Price (“Individual Bidder Portion”). All Bidders (except Anchor Investors) shall mandatorily participate in this Issue only through the
  Application Supported by Blocked Amount (“ASBA”) process and shall provide details of their respective bank account (including UPI ID (defined hereinafter) in case of UPI Bidders (defined
  hereinafter)) in which the Bid Amount will be blocked by the Self Certified Syndicate Banks (“SCSBs”) or the Sponsor Bank, as the case may be. Anchor Investors are not permitted to participate in
  the Anchor Investor Portion through the ASBA process. For further details, see “Issue Procedure” on page 360.

in the Equity Shares nor regarding the price at which the Equity Shares will be traded after listing.

                                       DEFINITIONS AND ABBREVIATIONS

This Draft Red Herring Prospectus uses certain definitions and abbreviations which, unless the context otherwise indicates
or implies or unless otherwise specified, shall have the meaning as provided below. References to any legislation, act,
regulations, rules, guidelines or policies shall be to such legislation, act, regulations, rules, guidelines or policies as
amended, supplemented, or re-enacted from time to time and any reference to a statutory provision shall include any
subordinate legislation made from time to time under that provision.

The words and expressions used in this Draft Red Herring Prospectus, but not defined herein shall have, to the extent
applicable, the meaning ascribed to such terms under SEBI ICDR Regulations, the Companies Act, the SCRA, the SEBI
LODR Regulations, the Depositories Act, and the rules and regulations made thereunder.

Notwithstanding the foregoing, the terms in “Basis for Issue Price”, “Statement of Special Tax Benefits”, “Industry
Overview”, “Key Regulations and Policies”, “Restated Consolidated Financial Information”, “Outstanding Litigation
and Material Developments”, “Issue Procedure” and “Main Provisions of the Articles of Association” on pages 125, 133,
136, 242, 285, 318, 360 and 381 respectively, shall have the meanings ascribed to such terms in the respective sections.

Our growth trajectory and business performance depends on the volume of tenders, project allocations, and capital
expenditure budgets of such government authorities, particularly in the power infrastructure, electrification, and engineering
sectors in which we operate. We cannot assure you that government policies at the Central or State level will continue to
prioritize infrastructure development or allocate adequate budgets for such projects. Any reduction, postponement, or
reprioritization of public spending including those arising from political transitions, elections, fiscal constraints, or policy
changes may directly impact the number of tenders floated and awarded. Government contracts typically involve longer
approval cycles, complex tendering processes, and stringent compliance requirements. These contracts are often governed
by standard terms favourable to the government, providing limited room for negotiation and imposing obligations such as
liquidated damages, strict performance timelines, and unilateral variation in scope of work. Such entities may also delay
payments due to procedural issues, budget release delays, or administrative bottlenecks, which could strain our working
capital and result in higher financing costs. Further, government bodies retain broad rights to suspend, terminate, or modify
contracts, with compensation or payment recovery often subject to lengthy processes or disputes. Mobilization for
additional or revised scope may require rapid deployment of resources, potentially increasing costs and affecting project
profitability. Our dependence on government and government-owned customers therefore exposes us to risks relating to
policy uncertainty, delays in project award, cost overruns, payment delays, and onerous contractual terms.

During the past, there have been two instances of pre-termination of contracts awarded to our Company by government
authorities, which illustrate the inherent risks associated with such engagements. In one instance, our Company has entered
into a Joint Venture Agreement with Denta Properties and Infrastructure Private Limited under the name Core4 Engineers–
DPIPL JV for execution of certain railway infrastructure works, the contract titled “Palakkad Division – Provision of new
6-metre-wide Foot Over Bridges connecting platforms and second entry at Angadipuram, Shoranur, Payyanur, Kasaragod
and Mangalore Junction stations under the Amrit Bharat Station Scheme (total five stations)” experienced a delay of
approximately 13 months, primarily due to factors attributable to the Government, including delays in approval of General
Arrangement drawings and failure to hand over sites required for commencement of work. Despite us bringing these issues
to the attention of the concerned authorities, the contract was terminated vide Termination Order No.
SR/PGT/Civil/2024/0110/RD-007 dated May 21, 2025. We have filed MA (Arb) No. 51 of 2025 under Section 23 of the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 before the District Court of Palakkad against the Union of India, acting through the
Senior Divisional Engineer (West), Palakkad Division, Southern Railway, challenging the said termination. The
proceedings, including the petition under Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 seeking injunction and
damages, are pending before the Hon’ble District Court at Palakkad. In another instance, disputes arose pursuant to the
termination of a contract titled “Provision of coach watering arrangements, drainage, water cisterns, platform benches and
signage boards at Mangalore.” In connection with the termination of this contract, our Company has filed an application
under Section 11(6) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 before the Hon’ble High Court of Karnataka against the
Union of India, acting through the Senior Divisional Engineer (West), Palakkad Division, Southern Railway, seeking
appointment of an arbitrator. This matter is also pending. For further details, also see “Outstanding Litigation and Material
Developments” on page 318.

The outcome of these proceedings is uncertain, and any adverse determination, delays in resolution, or inability to recover
amounts claimed may have an adverse effect on our cash flows, financial condition, and results of operations. Further,
recurrence of similar events in future government contracts could negatively impact our order book execution, profitability,
reputation, and ability to secure new contracts.

     Our geographic concentration exposes us to heightened risks arising from adverse regulatory, economic, demographic,
     political or social developments in Karnataka, including natural or man-made disasters, labour unrest, and changes in state
     taxation, duties, incentives or sector-specific policies. Any reduction in infrastructure spending or budgetary allocation in
     Karnataka, or a slowdown in construction activity in the state, could adversely impact our order inflow, revenues and
     profitability. However, any future unrest could disrupt project timelines, workforce availability, logistics and supply chains,
     and overall economic stability, thereby adversely affecting our business.

     Further, our brand presence is relatively regional. Expansion into other states may require us to establish new client
     relationships, comply with differing regulatory frameworks and compete with entrenched regional players. Any inability to
     successfully diversify our geographic footprint may exacerbate the risks associated with our concentration in Karnataka.
     Consequently, any adverse regional developments in Karnataka could materially and adversely affect our business, financial
     condition, results of operations, cash flows and growth prospects. Further, there have been no instances during the last 3
     financial years and current financial year where our Company has been impacted due to its revenue from the State of
     Karnataka or exposure to risks specific to these geographies and market conditions.

Projects included in our order book may be delayed, modified, put on hold, cancelled, or not fully paid for by customers
due to factors beyond our control, including funding constraints, customer defaults, delayed approvals, regulatory issues,
changes in project priorities, adverse macro-economic conditions, supply chain disruptions, and force majeure events. Such
delays may cause projects to remain in the order book for extended periods without significant execution progress. In cases
of cancellation or premature termination, we cannot assure recovery of termination payments in a timely manner or at
amounts that fully cover costs already incurred.

In addition, a significant portion of our projects are with government and public-sector clients, where contracts are awarded
through competitive tendering. These contracts are based on standard terms prescribed by the respective authorities and
may include conditions that adversely impact profitability, cash flows, and execution timelines. Government entities also
retain broad rights to cancel, modify, or suspend projects at any stage. Delays in certification, billing, or release of payments
under such contracts may further affect our working capital and financial position. Further, even in projects that proceed as
scheduled, revenue realization may vary from estimates due to variations in scope, re-measurement of quantities, and
adjustments under the contract terms. Delays expose us to the risk of cost overruns, increased working capital requirements,
and margin pressures.

During the past, there have been two instances of pre-termination of contracts awarded to our Company by government
authorities, which illustrate the inherent risks associated with such engagements. In one instance, Our Company has entered
into a Joint Venture Agreement with Denta Properties and Infrastructure Private Limited under the name Core4 Engineers–
DPIPL JV for execution of certain railway infrastructure works, the contract titled “Palakkad Division – Provision of new
6-metre-wide Foot Over Bridges connecting platforms and second entry at Angadipuram, Shoranur, Payyanur, Kasaragod
and Mangalore Junction stations under the Amrit Bharat Station Scheme (total five stations)” experienced a delay of
approximately 13 months, primarily due to factors attributable to the Government, including delays in approval of General
Arrangement drawings and failure to hand over sites required for commencement of work. Despite us bringing these issues
to the attention of the concerned authorities, the contract was terminated vide Termination Order No.
SR/PGT/Civil/2024/0110/RD-007 dated May 21, 2025. We have filed MA (Arb) No. 51 of 2025 under Section 23 of the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 before the District Court of Palakkad against the Union of India, acting through the
Senior Divisional Engineer (West), Palakkad Division, Southern Railway, challenging the said termination.The
proceedings, including the petition under Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 seeking injunction and
damages, are pending before the Hon’ble District Court at Palakkad. In another instance, disputes arose pursuant to the
termination of a contract titled “Provision of coach watering arrangements, drainage, water cisterns, platform benches and
signage boards at Mangalore.” In connection with the termination of this contract, our Company has filed an application
under Section 11(6) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 before the Hon’ble High Court of Karnataka against the
Union of India, acting through the Senior Divisional Engineer (West), Palakkad Division, Southern Railway, seeking
appointment of an arbitrator. This matter is also pending. For further details, also see “Outstanding Litigation and Material
Developments” on page 318.

     to risks such as changes in government priorities, delays in budget approvals, deferment or cancellation of projects,

     expenditure by the Government in the railway sector, including due to fiscal constraints, political changes, or
     macroeconomic conditions, could reduce the availability of new projects or delay execution of awarded contracts, thereby
     adversely affecting our order inflows and revenue visibility. Further, railway projects typically involve complex execution
     requirements, multiple layers of approvals, coordination with various government authorities, and dependency on timely
     handover of sites, drawings, and clearances. Delays or inefficiencies in any of these aspects may lead to time overruns, cost
     escalations, lower margins, and working capital strain. Additionally, railway contracts often contain stringent performance
     obligations, penalty clauses, and termination rights in favour of the awarding authority, which may expose us to financial
     and operational risks in the event of project delays or disputes.

     changes, safety-related directives, changes in technical specifications, or increased compliance requirements specific to the
     railway sector could increase project costs or affect execution timelines. Moreover, heightened competition within the
     railway infrastructure segment, including from larger EPC players or government-backed entities, may exert pressure on
     bid pricing and margins, affecting profitability.

7.   We are required to furnish performance guarantees as part of our business. Our inability to arrange for such guarantees
     or the invocation of such guarantees may adversely affect our cash flows and financial condition.

     In the ordinary course of our business, particularly in relation to infrastructure and government-awarded contracts, we are
     required to furnish various performance-related guarantees, including performance bank guarantees, mobilisation advance
     guarantees, retention money guarantees, and other financial assurances, in favour of our customers. These guarantees are
     typically issued by banks or financial institutions and are required to be maintained for the duration of the contract and, in
     certain cases, beyond the completion of the project until the expiry of defect liability or maintenance periods. As part of
     our business operations, we are mandatorily required to furnish performance-related bank guarantees for projects
     undertaken by us, particularly those awarded by government entities, public sector undertakings, and other institutional
     clients. Such guarantees generally include bid security, advance bank guarantees, performance bank guarantees, and
     retention guarantees. While the industry practice permits the aggregate bank guarantee requirement to extend up to
     approximately 30% of the contract value, our Company’s projects typically require furnishing bank guarantees limited to
     around 5% of the contract value.

     Our ability to procure such guarantees is dependent on several factors, including our credit profile, financial performance,
     net worth, banking relationships, collateral availability, and compliance with covenants imposed by lenders and issuing
     banks. Any deterioration in our financial condition, tightening of credit conditions, adverse changes in banking policies, or
     reduction in sanctioned limits may impair our ability to obtain or renew such guarantees on commercially acceptable terms
     or within required timelines. Failure to arrange or extend performance guarantees could result in disqualification from
     tenders, delays in commencement of projects, suspension of work, or termination of existing contracts, thereby adversely
     affecting our revenues and growth prospects. Further, performance guarantees may be invoked by customers in
     circumstances such as alleged delays in execution, disputes over quality or specifications, non-performance, or termination
     of contracts, including in situations where such invocation may be disputed by us. Invocation of guarantees would require
     immediate payment by the issuing bank, which may in turn require us to reimburse the bank or result in adjustment against
     cash margins or collateral. Such invocation could lead to significant cash outflows, increase our working capital
     requirements, adversely impact liquidity, and reduce funds available for ongoing operations and future projects.

     During the past, there have been two instances of pre-termination of contracts awarded to our Company by government
     authorities, which illustrate the inherent risks associated with such engagements. In one instance, Our Company has entered
     into a Joint Venture Agreement with Denta Properties and Infrastructure Private Limited under the name Core4 Engineers–

     Additionally, invocation or frequent utilisation of guarantees may adversely affect our banking relationships, credit ratings,

8.   Delays in completion of our current and future projects and time overrun could have adverse effect on our business
     prospects and results of operations.


                                                                  39
     Our EPC projects are typically governed by strict completion schedules, milestone-based execution requirements, and
     defined contractual timelines that are determined based on technical feasibility assessments and mutually agreed schedules
     with our clients. However, actual project execution is subject to a number of inherent risks and uncertainties, and completion
     may be delayed due to factors beyond our control. These include unforeseen site conditions, engineering or design
     complexities, delays in approval of drawings or technical specifications, force majeure events, changes or expansions in
     project scope, shortages or unavailability of skilled labour or construction materials, supply chain disruptions, delays in
     obtaining statutory or regulatory permissions, and financial, operational, or coordination challenges faced by our clients,
     vendors, or sub-contractors.

     As an EPC contractor, we are required to furnish bank guarantees, performance securities, and other contractual assurances
     for each project, which are generally required to remain valid until the completion of the project and, in certain cases,
     through the defect liability or maintenance period. Delays in project completion may require us to extend the validity of
     such guarantees and securities, resulting in additional costs, higher bank commissions, and prolonged blockage of credit
     limits or cash margins. In certain circumstances, project delays may also expose us to the risk of imposition of liquidated
     damages, encashment of performance guarantees, forfeiture of security deposits, or termination of contracts by clients,
     which could lead to immediate cash outflows and adversely affect our liquidity and financial position.

     While we have not experienced any material adverse consequences arising from project delays in the past, there can be no
     assurance that extensions of time will be granted in all cases or that liquidated damages, penalties, or other contractual
     remedies will not be imposed by clients in the future. The invocation of guarantees or imposition of penalties, even in cases
     where delays are attributable to factors beyond our control, could adversely affect our cash flows, banking relationships,
     credit profile, and ability to bid for or execute future projects.

     Further, delays in project execution typically result in cost overruns, including additional expenses related to labour,
     materials, equipment deployment, site overheads, supervision, financing costs, and working capital funding. In many
     contracts, the scope for recovery of such additional costs through escalation clauses, variation claims, or compensation for
     delays is limited or subject to prolonged negotiation or dispute resolution. Any inability to recover such incremental costs
     in a timely manner, or at all, may adversely impact our project-level margins, overall profitability, and cash flows.

     Accordingly, any significant delay, time overrun, or disruption in the execution of our current or future EPC projects could
     have a material adverse effect on our business operations, financial condition, results of operations, cash flows, and growth
     prospects.

9.   Premature termination of projects may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

     Our agreements with project owners, including government bodies, public sector undertakings, and private entities, are
     subject to premature termination under various circumstances. Such termination may arise due to factors including, but not
     limited to, failure to furnish, renew, or replenish performance securities or bank guarantees, delays in achievement of project
     milestones, alleged non-compliance with contractual terms or technical specifications, insolvency or financial distress,
     occurrence of force majeure events, abandonment or suspension of projects, disputes among promoters or management, or
     failure to adhere to prescribed work schedules, quality standards, safety requirements, or customer instructions. In certain
     cases, project owners may also have contractual rights to terminate projects for convenience by providing prior notice,
     without any default on our part.

     If any of the foregoing events occur, project owners may terminate our agreements in whole or in part, reduce the scope of
     work, suspend execution, or impose liquidated damages and other contractual remedies. Such actions may result in
     immediate cessation of project-related revenues and may require us to demobilize manpower, machinery, and equipment
     at short notice, leading to inefficiencies and additional costs. Further, premature termination may result in invocation of
     performance guarantees, forfeiture of security deposits, withholding of retention monies, or imposition of penalties, which
     could adversely affect our liquidity, working capital position, and banking arrangements.

     While in certain circumstances we may be contractually entitled to termination payments, compensation for work executed,
     or reimbursement of costs incurred, there can be no assurance that such payments will be received in a timely manner or
     that they will be adequate to cover all costs, including fixed overheads, equipment mobilisation and demobilisation costs,
     employee-related expenses, financing costs, and other project-specific expenditures. In some cases, recovery of such
     amounts may be subject to prolonged negotiations, dispute resolution proceedings, or arbitration, which may further strain
     our financial resources and management bandwidth.

     Additionally, premature termination of projects may adversely affect our reputation, track record, and perceived execution
     capability, which could impair our ability to qualify for or secure new projects, particularly in government or large
     infrastructure tenders where past performance and completion history are key evaluation criteria. Any such reputational
     impact may have a long-term adverse effect on our order inflows and growth prospects.

13. We undertake a portion of our work through sub-contracting arrangements, and our reliance on sub-contracting

    business, financial condition, and results of operations.

    We undertake a portion of our work through sub-contracting arrangements, in addition to executing projects directly as a
    main contractor. Sub-contracting arrangements are typically governed by contracts with primary contractors and may
    impose conditions, obligations, and performance standards that are more restrictive than those applicable to our direct
    contracts with project owners. Such conditions may include tighter timelines, limited scope for variation or escalation,
    stricter quality and safety standards, enhanced reporting requirements, back-to-back liability clauses, and limited rights to
    dispute or claim compensation for delays or cost overruns.

    The terms of such sub-contracts are largely determined by the primary contractor, and our ability to negotiate favourable
    contractual protections may be limited. Non-compliance with contractual obligations, whether due to factors within or
    beyond our control, may result in adverse consequences, including early termination of the sub-contract, imposition of
    penalties or liquidated damages, recovery of costs by the primary contractor, withholding of payments, or invocation of
    performance securities furnished by us. In certain cases, disputes or defaults by other sub-contractors or by the primary
    contractor itself may also adversely affect our performance, payments, or ability to complete our scope of work.

14. Our business is significantly dependent on the performance of the sectors in which our customers operate, and any
    downturn in such sectors may adversely affect our business, financial condition, results of operations, and cash flows.

    The commercial success of our business is closely linked to the performance, growth, and capital expenditure cycles of the
    sectors in which our customers operate. We primarily derive revenue from government bodies, state utilities, public sector
    undertakings, and institutional clients in the power transmission and distribution sector, water infrastructure sector, and
    railway infrastructure sector. The activity levels in these sectors are directly influenced by macroeconomic conditions,
    policy priorities, budgetary allocations, funding availability, and long-term infrastructure plans of the Central and State
    Governments.

    Any slowdown, deferral, or reduction in government spending, sector-specific reforms, or project tendering activity may
    adversely impact the number and size of projects awarded, thereby affecting our order inflow, revenue visibility, and overall
    business performance. For instance, delays in tariff approvals, funding constraints at utilities, administrative bottlenecks,
    or changes to state or central policies in the power distribution sector may lead to slower project execution and extended
    payment cycles. In the water infrastructure sector, variations in municipal or state-level budget allocations, regulatory
    changes, or delays in approvals may impact project timelines and demand for our services. Similarly, a slowdown in railway
    infrastructure expansion or a shift in government priorities could reduce opportunities for contractors and engineering
    service providers such as us.

    Our long-term business prospects also depend on the commercial viability and operational success of projects executed for
    our clients. If such projects face delays, funding shortages, or policy-driven restructuring, it may reduce follow-on
    opportunities and affect our ability to secure repeat business.

    Accordingly, any adverse developments, structural challenges, or cyclical downturns in the industries in which our end-use
    customers operate may materially and adversely affect our business, results of operations, financial condition, and cash
    flows.

15. Our actual costs in completing a project may vary significantly from the assumptions underlying our bid, and we may
    be unable to recover additional expenses, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, results of
    operations, and cash flows.

    The contract value for most of our EPC projects is determined based on estimates prepared at the bidding stage, which
    factor in anticipated costs of construction materials, fuel, labour, subcontractors, logistics, equipment utilisation, and site
    conditions. These estimates are derived from pre-bid assessments and market information available at that time. However,
    actual project execution costs may differ significantly from these assumptions due to various factors, including fluctuations
    in the prices of key raw materials such as steel, cement, electrical components, fuel, and consumables, variations in labour
    costs, changes in statutory compliances, delays in material supply, increased subcontracting charges, equipment repair or
    replacement costs, and other operational challenges.

    As our pre-bid studies including site reconnaissance, preliminary engineering assessments, and estimation of quantities are
    typically undertaken within compressed timelines, they may not always fully capture on-ground complexities. As a result,
    deviations from initial assumptions may arise during execution. In many cases, contracts do not permit full recovery of
    increased costs from clients, particularly where such overruns do not qualify as change-of-scope events. This may lead to
    reduced margins, working capital stress, and adverse liquidity impact.

    Further, if project cost overruns are significant, we may be required to arrange additional financing to meet such increased
    working capital needs. There can be no assurance that such financing will be available on favourable terms or at all. Any
    substantial or repeated cost overruns could materially and adversely affect our business, financial performance, cash flows,
    and overall results of operations.

16. We operate in a competitive industry and face certain competitive pressures from the existing competitors and new
    entrants in both public and private sector and we may not be successful in bidding and winning for projects to grow our
    business which could have material impact on our business operations.

    We operate in a highly competitive environment and face competition from a large number of established players as well
    as new entrants in both the public and private sectors. Our competitors include large, well-capitalized infrastructure and
    EPC companies, regional and sector-focused contractors, public sector undertakings, and government-backed entities, some
    of which may have greater financial resources, larger balance sheets, broader technical capabilities, longer operating
    histories, stronger brand recognition, or preferential access to funding, equipment, or skilled manpower.

                                                                  45
    Competition in our industry is primarily driven by price, technical capability, past execution track record, financial strength,
    compliance with eligibility criteria, and ability to meet stringent qualification requirements prescribed in tenders. In many
    cases, contracts are awarded through competitive bidding processes where the lowest or most competitive bid, subject to
    technical qualification, is selected. This may result in significant pricing pressure, reduced margins, and increased execution
    risk, particularly during periods of heightened competition or economic slowdown when bidders may adopt aggressive
    pricing strategies to secure limited project opportunities.

    Further, the infrastructure sector has relatively low entry barriers in certain segments, and new entrants, including joint
    ventures, consortiums, or entities backed by financial investors, may enter the market and intensify competition.
    Additionally, consolidation within the industry or the entry of international players through partnerships or subsidiaries
    may further increase competitive pressures. Our inability to effectively compete with such players on pricing, technical
    capability, or execution track record could result in loss of market share, reduced order inflows, or failure to secure projects
    necessary for sustaining and growing our operations.

    Our business growth depends significantly on our ability to successfully bid for and win new projects on commercially
    viable terms. There can be no assurance that we will be successful in securing future contracts at acceptable margins, or at
    all. Any sustained decline in our bid success rate or deterioration in pricing discipline could adversely affect our revenues,
    profitability, cash flows, and financial condition. Further, failure to win projects may result in underutilisation of resources,
    including manpower and equipment, thereby increasing fixed costs and reducing operational efficiency.

17. The industry in which we operate possess various risks and challenges as provided in the Industry Report titled “India’s
    Railway EPC, Drinking Water & Waste Water Treatment, Transmission & Distribution, Power Distribution Panels &
    Compact Sub-Stations, and SCADA & Automation Systems Market” published on February 19, 2026, which is
    exclusively prepared for the purposes of the Issue and issued by Ken Research and is commissioned and paid for by our
    Company (“Ken Report”).

    The EPC Industry in which we operate possess various risks and challenges such as:

    India’s Railway EPC Market:

        •    Payment delays straining working capital and slowing project execution: Financial challenges stem from
             payment delays and high bank guarantees that lock up working capital. Indian Railways contracts allow monthly
             billing based on verified work, but no advance payments and multi-level approvals often cause significant payment
             lags.

        •    Design and Engineering Risks: Frequent design revisions, incomplete surveys, and delayed approvals from rail
             authorities lead to rework, idle resources, and extended timelines.

        •    Price Volatility of Steel, Cement, and Copper Inputs: Sharp fluctuations in key input prices erode margins
             under fixed-price contracts despite escalation clauses, as costs of steel, copper, cement, and aggregates often surge
             unpredictably, straining cash flows and project profitability.

        •    Restricted Site Access on Live Tracks Complicating Execution and Civil Works in Dense Corridors:
             Execution on live tracks is constrained by short block windows (2–3 hours), requiring rapid work under tight safety
             protocols. In dense corridors, limited space, underground utilities, and encroachments further hinder civil works
             and resource coordination.

        •    Elongated Supply chain: Multiple subcontractors and long lead times for fabricated and electrical components
             disrupt project schedules and increase logistics complexity, as coordination across suppliers, testing agencies, and
             transport networks often leads to delays, rework, and cost overruns in large, multi-location railway EPC projects.

    India’s Drinking Water and Waste Water Market:

        •    Operational Inefficiencies: Skills shortages, outdated assets, and inefficient processes reduce uptime and
             compliance, increasing project risks and execution costs for EPC players.

        •    High Capex and Maintenance Costs: Building treatment plants involves heavy upfront investment in pumps,
             filtration systems, pipelines, and compliance infrastructure. Ongoing O&M expenses such as energy-intensive
             operations, skilled staffing, and equipment upgrades strain financial viability.



                                                                   46
        •    Residuals Handling & Disposal: Sludge, screenings, and RO concentrate need compliant dewatering, transport,
             and disposal; limited landfill/incineration options and permits create bottlenecks and shutdown risk.

        •    Delays in Land Acquisition & Clearances: Development of water and wastewater treatment plants is highly
             dependent on timely land allocation and environmental approvals. Local disputes, lack of clarity in regulatory
             processes, or extended permit reviews can stall construction, increase financing costs, and disrupt project
             timelines.

    India’s Power Distribution Panels and Compact Substation Market:

        •    Dependence on Tender-Based Procurement: A large share of demand comes from government and utility
             projects, making the market heavily tender-driven. This results in long approval cycles, high competition, and
             margin pressures, impacting revenue predictability and timelines.

        •    Excessive Expenditure on Heat Management: High temperatures and compact enclosures cause overheating
             and equipment failure; requires proper ventilation and derating. This causes inefficiencies and reduces
             profitability.

        •    Cost Pressures: Escalating prices of copper, steel, and other metals, combined with additional expenses for
             product certification, safety testing, and site-specific customization, significantly squeeze margins.

        •    Safety and Reliability Risks: Arc-flash incidents, poor earthing practices, and water ingress remain
             persistent risks that can lead to major equipment failures, power outages, and worker injuries.

    India’s Transmission and Distribution Market:

        •    Dependence on Tender-Based Procurement: Most T&D projects are utility-led, involving lengthy bid cycles,
             intense price competition, and thin margins. Delayed awards and strict qualification norms further strain cash
             flows and limit flexibility for EPC players.

        •    Weak Financial Health of DISCOMs: Chronic payment delays, mounting subsidy backlogs, and unresolved
             tariff gaps strain contractor cash flows and escalate financing costs. In several cases, this has led contractors to
             pursue prolonged legal or arbitration proceedings, tying up working capital and disrupting execution timelines.

        •    Right-of-Way (RoW) & Clearance Delays: Land disputes and slow environmental approvals frequently stall
             transmission projects and extend timelines.

    India’s SCADA and Automation Systems Market:

        •    High Capital Cost and Integration Complexity: It requires upfront investment in hardware, software licenses,
             cybersecurity frameworks, and networking infrastructure. Integration with legacy systems adds technical
             challenges and cost burdens, slowing adoption.

        •    Shortage of Skilled Technicians: SCADA deployment and maintenance demand specialized expertise in both
             operational technology (OT) and information technology (IT). A shortage of trained personnel delays
             implementation increases dependency on third parties.

        •    Cybersecurity Risks: SCADA and automation systems are prime targets for cyberattacks. Successful breaches
             can halt operations, manipulate critical controls, compromise sensitive operational data, and threaten safety.

    These above challenges could have a material adverse effect on our business, financial condition, cash flow and results of
    operations.

20. We have a high working capital requirement, and our Company proposes to utilize ₹3,268.00 lakhs of the Net Proceeds
    towards our incremental net working capital requirements for Fiscal 2027. The actual amount and timing of our future
    working capital requirements may differ from estimates as a result of, among other factors, unforeseen delays,
    unanticipated expenses, regulatory changes, economic conditions and market developments. If we are unable to raise
    sufficient working capital, our operations may be adversely affected.

    We are engaged in the business of providing infrastructure and engineering solutions across the power distribution, water
    and wastewater, automation, and utility infrastructure sectors. Each project typically uses both fund-based and non-fund-
    based banking facilities to meet its working capital requirements. Fund-based facilities provide the necessary cash flow to
    cover operating expenses, while non-fund-based facilities such as bank guarantees, performance guarantees etc. are offered
    as security under bid terms and are crucial for securing contracts and ensuring financial credibility. In most of the projects,
    our Company is required to furnish bank guarantees to customers as part of contractual terms. For securing bank guarantees,
    our Company needs to provide cash margin and eligible collateral. The requirement to set aside incremental cash margins
    for additional contracts contributes to the overall need for higher working capital. As a result of the above, we have a
    continuous, working capital requirement.

    The credit period offered by our customer is generally longer than what we are granted by our business partners and
    suppliers. Currently, we meet our working capital requirements through a mix of internal accruals and working capital
    facilities from scheduled commercial banks and TReDS limits. As on September 30, 2025, we had sanctioned working
    capital facilities aggregating ₹1,400.00 lakhs of which ₹ 1,050.42 lakhs are outstanding. We cannot assure you that we will
    continue to generate sufficient internal accruals and / or be able to raise adequate working capital from lenders to address
    our future needs. Our inability to meet our present or enhanced working capital requirements will have an adverse impact

                                                                  49
    on our results of operation, business and financial condition. For further details pertaining to our present working capital
    position, please see sections titled “Financial Indebtedness” and “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial
    Condition and Results of Operations” on pages 315 and 289, respectively.

26. Any future penalties or demands raised by statutory authorities may adversely impact the financial position of the

    labour laws, including timely filing and payment of GST, Employees’ Provident Fund (“EPF”), Employees’ State Insurance
    (“ESI”), and Tax Deducted at Source (“TDS”). These filings are governed by the Central Goods and Services Tax Act,
    2017, the Employees’ Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948,

    even prosecution. For instance, non-payment or delayed payment of GST can attract interest under Section 50 of the CGST
    Act and penalties under Section 122. Similarly, failure to deposit EPF and ESI contributions within prescribed timelines
    may result in damages, penalties, and legal action from the respective enforcement authorities. TDS defaults, including
    non-deduction, short deduction, or delayed payment, can also lead to disallowance of expenses, interest under Section 201,
    and penalties under the Income Tax Act.

27. We have unsecured loans outstanding from our Directors and Promoters, which may be recalled at any time and could
    adversely affect our financial condition.

    We have unsecured loans outstanding from our Promoters and Directors, which may be recalled at any time and could
    adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. As of September 30, 2025, we had unsecured
    loans outstanding from our Promoters and Directors aggregating to ₹274.49 lakhs. These loans have been availed to meet
    our business requirements from time to time. The terms of such loans are not governed by detailed loan agreements, are not
    secured against any of our assets, and generally do not carry fixed repayment schedules. Consequently, such loans may be
    repayable on demand, subject to applicable laws.

    Since these loans have been provided by our Promoters and Directors, they are not considered to be on arm’s length terms.
    There can be no assurance that our Promoters and Directors will not seek repayment of these loans at short notice. If such
    repayment is demanded, we may be required to arrange funds at short notice, either from our internal accruals or by raising
    debt or equity financing, which may not be available on favourable terms, or at all. This could adversely impact our liquidity,
    strain our cash flows and materially affect our ability to fund our operations and growth initiatives.

    Further, reliance on unsecured loans from our Promoters and Directors may give rise to a perception of financial
    dependence, which could negatively affect investor confidence and our ability to raise external financing. In the event we
    are unable to replace such funding with borrowings from banks, financial institutions, or other investors on acceptable
    terms, our business operations, financial condition, and results of operations may be materially and adversely affected.

29. A pending civil litigation against our Company as disclosed under the pending matters, which, if they result in an adverse
    outcome, would materially and adversely affect the operations or the financial position of our Company.

    A civil litigation is pending against us, where no amount is involved against our Company and hence the impact of this
    case in the future is not quantifiable till date. The litigation has been disclosed as a pending matters in the chapter titled


                                                                                         56
    “Outstanding Litigation and Material Developments” on page 318, which, if they result in an adverse outcome, would
    materially and adversely affect the operations or the financial position of our Company. While the matter is not considered
    material, any adverse outcome may result in financial liabilities, including outflows of cash, which could have an impact
    our financial position and results of operations. The disclosure of the pending civil litigation is as follows:

    An e-tender bearing no. 3SBC23 of 21-09-2023 Item 5, dated September 21, 2023 (the “Tender”), was floated by the
    Senior Divisional Engineer (Co-ord) SBC, South Western Railway (the “Respondent No. 1”) for the proposed provision
    of coach watering facilities at Kengeri Station. Pushkraj Crushing Equipment Private Limited (the “Petitioner”) and our
    Company were the L1 and L2, respectively, in the bidding process. It was later observed by Respondent No. 1 that the
    Petitioner did not qualify under the prior experience and turnover criteria, as stipulated in the Tender. Accordingly, a
    termination notice was issued by Respondent No. 1 to the Petitioner, and the construction work was awarded to our
    Company vide Letter of Acceptance bearing no. BANGALORE DIVISION – ENGG 13SBC23 21-09-2023 Item
    5/10811020101567, dated April 23, 2024, pursuant to which the contract for the construction works was awarded to our
    Company for a total contract value of ₹229.37 lakhs.

    Aggrieved by this, the Petitioner filed a Civil Writ Petition bearing no. WP/26134/2023 (the “Writ Petition”) before the
    Karnataka High Court, Principal Bench at Bengaluru (the “Hon’ble High Court”), against Respondent No. 1 and our
    Company. Since our Company has no connection with the termination of the Petitioner, our Company filed a petition dated
    December 17, 2025, before the Hon’ble High Court seeking deletion of its name from the Writ Petition.

    opposition by third parties or if any injunctive or other adverse order is issued against us in respect of our trademark, we

    third parties, which may adversely affect our goodwill and business.

32. Non-compliance with and changes in any of the applicable laws, rules or regulations may adversely affect our business,
    results of operations and financial condition and cash flows.

    We operate across multiple infrastructure verticals, including railway EPC, drinking water and wastewater treatment, power
    transmission and distribution, manufacture and supply of electrical panels and compact substations, and SCADA and
    automation systems. Our operations are subject to a wide range of central, state and local laws, regulations, policies,
    guidelines and technical standards governing project design, procurement, execution, commissioning and operations,


                                                                 58
    including those issued by Indian Railways, electricity authorities and regulators, environmental and water authorities, and
    other governmental bodies.

    Our railway EPC operations are governed by the Railways Act, 1989, Railway Board circulars and manuals, public
    procurement norms and contractual frameworks, while our drinking water and wastewater treatment projects are regulated
    under environmental and water laws. Our power transmission and distribution, panel manufacturing and substation
    activities are governed by the Electricity Act, 2003 and regulations issued by the Central Electricity Authority and electricity
    regulatory commissions, and our SCADA and automation solutions are subject to applicable technical, grid safety and
    cybersecurity standards. These laws and regulations impose stringent requirements relating to safety, quality, timelines,
    cost controls, environmental compliance and operational standards.

    In addition, we are subject to labour, employment, health and safety, environmental, taxation and other general laws, which
    are subject to frequent changes and varying interpretations and enforcement practices. Our operations involve deployment
    of a significant workforce, and are subject to laws relating to minimum wages, social security contributions, occupational
    safety and working conditions. Any non-compliance, delay in obtaining or renewing approvals, changes in regulatory
    requirements, or adverse regulatory action may result in inspections, penalties, demands, litigation, liquidated damages,
    increased compliance costs, project delays, termination of contracts, blacklisting, remediation obligations or revocation of
    approvals, and could result in reputational harm.

    Compliance with these requirements may involve significant costs, and increased regulatory enforcement, stricter
    environmental or safety standards, or claims arising from property damage, environmental harm or personal injury may

    condition, results of operations and prospects.

58. Pursuant to listing of the Equity Shares, we may be subject to pre-emptive surveillance measures like Additional
    Surveillance Measure (ASM) and Graded Surveillance Measures (GSM) by the Stock Exchange in order to enhance
    market integrity and safeguard the interest of investors.

    SEBI and the Stock Exchanges have introduced various pre-emptive surveillance measures in order to enhance market
    integrity and safeguard the interests of investors, including ASM, GSM and ESM. These measures are imposed on securities
    of companies based on various objective criteria such as significant variations in price and volume, concentration of certain
    client accounts as a percentage of combined trading volume, average delivery, or where the trading price of securities
    witnesses an abnormal rise not commensurate with the financial health and fundamentals of such company, including
    parameters such as earnings, book value, fixed assets, net worth, price/earnings multiple and market capitalization. Under

                                                                 69
    the refined ESM framework, securities may also be placed under enhanced surveillance if they display abnormal price
    movement and are either loss-making or trading at valuations significantly higher than broad market benchmarks.

    Upon listing, the trading of our Equity Shares would be subject to differing market conditions as well as other factors which
    may result in high volatility in price, low trading volumes, and a large concentration of client accounts as a percentage of
    combined trading volume of our Equity Shares. The occurrence of any of the abovementioned factors or other circumstances
    may trigger any of the parameters prescribed by SEBI and the Stock Exchanges for placing our securities under the ASM,
    GSM or ESM framework or any other surveillance measures, which could result in significant restrictions on trading of our
    Equity Shares being imposed by SEBI and the Stock Exchanges. These restrictions may include requiring higher margin
    requirements, settlement on a trade-for-trade basis without netting, limiting trading frequency (for example, trading only
    once in a week or month), reduction of applicable price band, settlement on a gross basis, freezing of price on the upper
    side of trading, as well as mention of our Equity Shares on the surveillance dashboards of the Stock Exchanges. The
    imposition of such restrictions and curbs on trading may have an adverse effect on the market price, trading and liquidity
    of our Equity Shares and on the reputation and perception of our Company.

61. We may be affected by competition law in India and any adverse application or interpretation of the Competition Act
    may in turn adversely affect our business.

    The Competition Act, 2002, as amended (the “Competition Act”) was enacted for the purpose of preventing practices that
    have or are likely to have an adverse effect on competition in India and has mandated the Competition Commission of India
    to prevent such practices. The Competition Act has been recently amended pursuant to Companies (Amendment) Act, 2023,
    which has, inter-alia increased the scope of agreements to be reviewed by the Competition Commission of India and
    reporting of transaction to Competition Commission of India will be based on deal value of acquisition, merger or
    amalgamation, instead on asset or turnover. Under the Competition Act, any arrangement, understanding or action, whether
    formal or informal, which causes or is likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition is void and attracts
    substantial penalties. Further, any agreement among competitors which, directly or indirectly, involves determination of
    purchase or sale prices, limits or controls production, or shares the market by way of geographical area or number of
    subscribers in the relevant market is presumed to have an appreciable adverse effect in the relevant market in India and
    shall be void. The Competition Act also prohibits abuse of a dominant position by any enterprise.

    The Competition Act aims to, among other things, prohibit all agreements and transactions which may have an appreciable
    adverse effect in India. Consequently, all agreements entered into by us could be within the purview of the Competition
    Act. Further, the CCI has extra-territorial powers and can investigate any agreements, abusive conduct or combination
    occurring outside of India if such agreement, conduct or combination has an appreciable adverse effect in India. However,
    the impact of the provisions of the Competition Act on the agreements entered into by us cannot be predicted with certainty
    at this stage. We are not currently party to any outstanding proceedings, nor have we received notice in relation to non-
    compliance with the Competition Act or the agreements entered into by us. However, if we are affected, directly or
    indirectly, by the application or interpretation of any provision of the Competition Act, or any enforcement proceedings
    initiated by the CCI, or any adverse publicity that may be generated due to scrutiny or prosecution by the CCI or if any
    prohibition or substantial penalties are levied under the Competition Act, it may adversely affect our business, financial
    condition, cash flows, results of operations and prospects.

    affect our business, prospects and results of operations.

    Sanhita, 2023 and Bhartiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, which have replaced the Indian Penal Code, 1860, Code of Criminal

63. Under Indian law, foreign investors are subject to investment restrictions that limit our ability to attract foreign investors,
    which may adversely affect the trading price of the Equity Shares.

    Under foreign exchange regulations currently in force in India, transfer of shares between non-residents and residents are
    freely permitted (subject to compliance with sectoral norms and certain other exceptions), if they comply with the pricing
    guidelines and reporting requirements specified by the RBI. If a transfer of shares, which are sought to be transferred, is
    not in compliance with such requirements and fall under any of the exceptions specified by the RBI, then the RBI’s prior
    approval is required. Additionally, shareholders who seek to convert Rupee proceeds from a sale of shares in India into
    foreign currency and repatriate that foreign currency from India require a no-objection or a tax clearance certificate from
    the Indian income tax authorities. We cannot assure you that any required approval from the RBI or any other governmental
    agency can be obtained on any particular terms or at all.

    In addition, pursuant to the Press Note No. 3 (2020 Series), dated April 17, 2020, issued by the DPIIT, which has been
    incorporated as the proviso to Rule 6(a) of the FEMA Rules, investments where the beneficial owner of the equity shares
    is situated in or is a citizen of a country which shares a land border with India, can only be made through the Government
    approval route, as prescribed in the Consolidated FDI Policy dated October 15, 2020 and the FEMA Rules. Further, in the
    event of transfer of ownership of any existing or future foreign direct investment in an entity in India, directly or indirectly,
    resulting in the beneficial ownership falling within the aforesaid restriction/purview, such subsequent change in the
    beneficial ownership will also require approval of the Government of India. These investment restrictions shall also apply
    to subscribers of offshore derivative instruments. We cannot assure investors that any required approval from the RBI or
    any other governmental agency can be obtained on any particular terms or conditions or at all. For further information, see
    “Restrictions on Foreign Ownership of Indian Securities” on page 380.

64. Rights of shareholders under Indian laws may be more limited than under the laws of other jurisdictions.

    Indian legal principles related to corporate procedures, directors’ fiduciary duties and liabilities, and shareholders’ rights
    may differ from those that would apply to a company in another jurisdiction. Shareholders’ rights including in relation to
    class actions, under Indian law may not be as extensive as shareholders’ rights under the laws of other countries or
    jurisdictions. Investors may have more difficulty in asserting their rights as shareholder in an Indian company than as
    shareholder of a corporation in another jurisdiction.

65. A third party could be prevented from acquiring control of us post this Issue, because of anti-takeover provisions under
    Indian law.

    As a listed Indian entity, there are provisions in Indian law that may delay, deter or prevent a future takeover or change in
    control of our Company. Under the SEBI SAST Regulations, an acquirer has been defined as any person who, directly or
    indirectly, acquires or agrees to acquire shares or voting rights or control over a company, whether individually or acting
    in concert with others. Although these provisions have been formulated to ensure that interests of investors/shareholders
    are protected, these provisions may also discourage a third party from attempting to take control of our Company subsequent
    to completion of the Issue. Consequently, even if a potential takeover of our Company would result in the purchase of the
    Equity Shares at a premium to their market price or would otherwise be beneficial to our shareholders, such a takeover may
    not be attempted or consummated because of SEBI SAST Regulations.

    Equity Shares.

    Under current Indian tax laws, unless specifically exempted, capital gains arising from the sale of equity shares in an Indian
    company is generally taxable in India. Investors may be subject to payment of long-term or short-term capital gains tax in
    India, in addition to payment of Securities Transaction Tax (“STT”), on the sale of any Equity Shares held for more or less
    than 12 months immediately preceding the date of transfer. While non-residents may claim tax treaty benefits in relation to
    such capital gains income, generally, Indian tax treaties do not limit India’s right to impose a tax on capital gains arising
    from the sale of shares of an Indian company.

    In terms of the Finance Act (No.2), 2024, with effect from August 16, 2024, taxes payable by an assessee on the capital
    gains arising from transfer of long-term capital assets (introduced as Section 112A of the Income-Tax Act, 1961) shall be
    calculated on such long-term capital gains at the rate of 12.50%, where the long-term capital gains exceed ₹1.25 lakhs. The
    stamp duty for transfer of certain securities, other than debentures, on a delivery basis is currently specified at 0.015% and
    on a non-delivery basis is specified at 0.003% of the consideration amount. Also, the Government of India has announced
    the Union Budget for Fiscal 2027, pursuant to which the Finance Bill, 2026, introduced various amendments to taxation
    laws in India. The Finance Bill has been passed by Lok Sabha on March 25, 2026 and awaits final assent from the President
    of India to become law, and to be enacted as the Finance Act, 2026. We cannot predict whether any amendments made
    pursuant to such Finance Bill, 2026 or Finance Act, 2026 would have an adverse effect on our business and operations or
    on the industry in which we operate. Further, the GoI has enacted the Income Tax Act, 2025, which becomes effective April
    1, 2026, which introduces a new “tax year”, consolidates and restructures compliance, expands digital-first administration,
    and clarifies the scope of virtual digital assets and digital record-keeping. While the reform aims to simplify administration
    without changing tax rates, the transition may create interpretive uncertainty and require changes to our systems, controls,
    contracts, and processes in India. Failure to implement timely changes or accurately comply with could result in higher tax
    liabilities, cash flow timing impacts from withholding, interest and penalties, increased administrative costs, and disputes.
    Additional rules, notifications, or technology requirements issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes could be extensive
    or retrospective and may affect our Indian operations, subsidiaries, and cross-border arrangements. Any of the foregoing
    could adversely affect our business, financial condition, results of operations, and cash flow. Bidders are advised to consult
    their own tax advisors to understand their tax liability as per the laws prevailing on the date of disposal of Equity Shares.

    Under the Finance Act 2020, any dividends paid by an Indian company will be subject to tax in the hands of the shareholders
    at applicable rates. Such taxes will be withheld by the Indian company paying dividends. The Company may or may not
    grant the benefit of a tax treaty (where applicable) to a non-resident shareholder for the purposes of deducting tax at source
    pursuant to any corporate action including dividends. Investors are advised to consult their own tax advisors and to carefully
    consider the potential tax consequences of owning Equity Shares. Unfavourable changes in or interpretations of existing,
    or the promulgation of new, laws, rules and regulations including foreign investment and stamp duty laws governing our
    business and operations could result in us being deemed to be in contravention of such laws and may require us to apply
    for additional approvals.

                                                                                                     74
72. QIBs, Non-Institutional Bidders and Individual Bidders are not permitted to withdraw or lower their Bids (in terms of
    quantity of Equity Shares or the Bid Amount) at any stage after submitting a Bid.

    Pursuant to the SEBI ICDR Regulations, QIBs, Non-Institutional Bidders and Individual Bidders are required to pay the
    Bid Amount on submission of the Bid and are not permitted to withdraw or lower their Bids (in terms of quantity of Equity
    Shares or the Bid Amount) at any stage after submitting a Bid. While our Company is required to complete all necessary
    formalities for listing and commencement of trading of the Equity Shares on the Stock Exchange where such Equity Shares
    are proposed to be listed including Allotment pursuant to the Issue within such period as may be prescribed under applicable
    law, events affecting the Bidders’ decision to invest in the Equity Shares, including adverse changes in international or
    national monetary policy, financial, political or economic conditions, our business, results of operation or financial
    condition may arise between the date of submission of the Bid and Allotment. Our Company may complete the Allotment
    of the Equity Shares even if such events occur, and such events limit the Bidders’ ability to sell the Equity Shares Allotted
    pursuant to the Issue or cause the trading price of the Equity Shares to decline on listing.

73. Holders of Equity Shares could be restricted in their ability to exercise pre-emptive rights under Indian law and could
    thereby suffer future dilution of their ownership position.

    Under the Companies Act, a company having share capital and incorporated in India must offer holders of its Equity Shares
    pre-emptive rights to subscribe and pay for a proportionate number of Equity Shares to maintain their existing ownership
    percentages prior to the issuance of any new equity shares, unless the pre-emptive rights have been waived by the adoption
    of a special resolution. However, if the laws of the jurisdiction that you are in does not permit the exercise of such pre-
    emptive rights without our filing an offering document or registration statement with the applicable authority in such
    jurisdiction, you will be unable to exercise such pre-emptive rights unless we make such a filing. To the extent that you are
    unable to exercise pre-emptive rights granted in respect of the Equity Shares, you may suffer future dilution of your
    ownership position and your proportional interests in our Company would be reduced.

74. Future issuances or sales of Equity Shares, or convertible securities or other equity-linked securities could adversely
    affect the trading price of the Equity Shares.

    Our future issuances of Equity Shares, convertible securities or securities linked to the Equity Shares by us (including under
    employee stock option plans) or the disposal of Equity Shares by our Promoters or any of our other principal shareholders
    or the perception that such issuance or sales may occur, including to comply with the minimum public shareholding norms
    applicable to listed companies in India, may significantly affect the trading price of the Equity Shares and our ability to
    raise capital through an issue of our securities. There can be no assurance that we will not issue further Equity Shares or
    that the shareholders will not dispose of, pledge or otherwise encumber the Equity Shares. Any future issuances could also
    dilute the value of your investment in our Company.

75. Fluctuation in the exchange rate of the Rupee and other currencies could have an adverse effect on the value of our
    Equity Shares, independent of our operating results.

    Subject to requisite approvals, on listing, our Equity Shares will be quoted in Rupees on the Stock Exchange. Any dividends,
    if declared, in respect of our Equity Shares will be paid in Rupees and subsequently converted into the relevant foreign
    currency for repatriation, if required. Any adverse movement in exchange rates during the time that it takes to undertake
    such conversion may reduce the net dividend to such investors. In addition, any adverse movement in exchange rates during
    a delay in repatriating the proceeds from a sale of Equity Shares outside India, for example, because of a delay in regulatory
    approvals that may be required for the sale of Equity Shares may reduce the net proceeds received by shareholders.

    The exchange rate of the Rupee has changed substantially in the last two decades and could fluctuate substantially in the
    future, which may have a material adverse effect on the value of the Equity Shares and returns from the Equity Shares,
    independent of our operating results.

76. There is no guarantee that our Equity Shares will be listed on the BSE SME Platform in a timely manner or at all.

    In accordance with Indian law and practice, permission for listing and trading of our Equity Shares will not be granted until
    after certain actions have been completed in relation to this Issue and until Allotment of Equity Shares pursuant to this
    Issue. In accordance with current regulations and circulars issued by SEBI, our Equity Shares are required to be listed on
    the BSE SME within such time as mandated under UPI Circulars, subject to any change in the prescribed timeline in this
    regard. However, we cannot assure you that the trading in our Equity Shares will commence in a timely manner or at all.
    Any failure or delay in obtaining final listing and trading approvals may restrict your ability to dispose of your Equity
    Shares.


                                                                 75
77. Investors will not be able to sell immediately on an Indian stock exchange any of the Equity Shares they purchase in the
    Issue.

    Subject to requisite approvals, the Equity Shares will be listed on the Stock Exchange. Pursuant to applicable Indian laws,
    certain actions must be completed before the Equity Shares can be listed and trading in the Equity Shares may commence.
    Investors’ book entry, or ‘demat’ accounts with depository participants in India, are expected to be credited within one
    working day of the date on which the Basis of Allotment is approved by the Stock Exchange. The Allotment of Equity
    Shares in this Issue and the credit of such Equity Shares to the applicant’s demat account with depository participant could
    take approximately two Working Days from the Bid/ Issue Closing Date and trading in the Equity Shares upon receipt of
    final listing and trading approvals from the Stock Exchange is expected to commence within three Working Days of the
    Bid/ Issue Closing Date. There could be a failure or delay in listing of the Equity Shares on the Stock Exchange. Any failure
    or delay in obtaining the approval or otherwise commence trading in the Equity Shares would restrict investors’ ability to
    dispose of their Equity Shares. There can be no assurance that the Equity Shares will be credited to investors’ demat
    accounts, or that trading in the Equity Shares will commence, within the time periods specified in this risk factor. We could
    also be required to pay interest at the applicable rates if allotment is not made, refund orders are not dispatched or demat
    credits are not made to investors within the prescribed time periods. For further details, see “Issue Procedure” on page 360.

                                              GENERAL INFORMATION

Our Company was originally formed as a partnership firm under the name and style “Core4 Engineers” in Mysore,
Karnataka, under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, pursuant to a partnership deed dated June 16, 2014, as amended from
time to time and was registered with the Registrar of Firms, Mysore on July 11, 2014. Subsequently, the partnership firm
was converted into a private limited “Core4 Engineers Private Limited” on February 03, 2022 pursuant to the provisions
of Chapter XXI of the Companies Act, 2013 and a fresh Certificate of Incorporation dated February 03, 2022 was issued
by the Registrar of Companies, Central Registration Centre. Thereafter, our company was converted from a private limited
company to a public limited company, pursuant to a special resolution passed in the extraordinary general meeting of our
shareholders held on February 27, 2025 and the name of our Company was changed to “Core4 Engineers Limited” with a
fresh certificate of incorporation dated April 23, 2025, issued to our Company by the Assistant Registrar of
Companies/Deputy Registrar of Companies/ Registrar of Companies, Central Processing Centre.

the Regulation 32 of the SEBI LODR Regulations, our Company shall furnish to the Stock Exchange on a half yearly basis,
