SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICY AND NOTES TO THE RESTATED SUMMARY STATEMENTS                                                                                                                  ANNEXURE- 4


A. BACKGROUND
The Company is a Private Limited Company having CIN:U45309KA2022PLC157463 incorporated on 03-02-2022 under the provisions of the Companies Act 2013, and having its registered office at
No.12, 1st Floor, Near Ramana Maharshi Gyana Kendra, Next to New court, 'K' Block, Kuvempunagar, Mysore, Karnataka, India, 570023
The Company is presently engaged in offering its EPC services to Indian Railways, which is undergoing a massive development phase expected to continue for a minimum of 10 years. CORE4 also
possesses expertise in water and wastewater treatment technology, emphasizing zero liquid discharge. The company is competent in carrying out Extra High Voltage
(220KV/110KV/66KV/27KV/11KV) transmission and distribution work. Currently, it is executing projects for Karnataka State Power Transmission Company (KPTCL), Karnataka Urban Water
Supply and Drainage Board (KUWSDB) and private manufacturing companies such as Kayens Technologies Ltd. Additionally, CORE4 has integrated manufacturing facilities for the design,
construction and manufacture of HT/LT distribution panels, compact substations and SCADA-based automation panels. This capacity is a key factor enabling the company to deliver its HT/LT
distribution project services in a faster and more reliable manner, ensuring time-bound execution. All panels are type-tested by the Central Power Research Institute (CPRI).



Significant Accounting Policies
Basis of preparation:
The restated statement of assets and liabilities of the Company as at September 30, 2025, March 31, 2025, March 31, 2024 and March 31, 2023, the restated statement of profits and loss for the period
ended September 30, 2025, year ended March 31, 2025, March 31, 2024 and March 31, 2023 and cash flows for the period ended September 30, 2025, year ended March 31, 2025, March 31, 2024
and March 31, 2023 herein collectively referred to as ("Restated Financial Information") have been compiled by the management from the audited Financial Statements of the Company for the period
ended on September 30, 2025, year ended March 31, 2025, March 31, 2024 and March 31, 2023 approved by the Board of Directors of the Company. Restated Financial Information have been
prepared to comply in all material respects with the provisions of Part I of Chapter III of the Companies Act, 2013 ('the Act') read with Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules,
2014, Securities and Exchange Board of India (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018 (“ICDR Regulations”) issued by Securities and Exchange Board of India ('SEBI') and
Guidance note on Reports in Companies Prospectuses (Revised 2019) (“Guidance Note”). Restated financial information have been prepared specifically for inclusion in the Draft Red Herring
Prospectus ('DRHP') to be filed by the Company with the SME platform of BSE Limited ('BSE SME') in connection with its proposed Small and Medium Enterprise Initial Pubic Offer ('SME IPO').
The Company’s management has recast the Financial Statements in the form required by Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013 for the purpose of restated financial information. The preparation and
presentation of Financial Statements in conformity with the Indian GAAP, requires the management to make judgements, estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of revenues,
expenses, assets and liabilities and the disclosure of contingent liabilities, at the end of reporting period. Although these estimates are based on management's best knowledge of current events and
actions, uncertainty about these assumptions and estimates could result in outcomes requiring a material adjustment to the carrying amounts of assets or liabilities in future periods.
The restated financial information has been prepared and presented under historical cost convention on the accrual basis of accounting in accordance with the Generally Accepted Accounting Principles
in India (“GAAP”) and comply with the mandatory Accounting Standards (“AS”) specified under section 133 of the Companies Act 2013, read with Rule 7 of the Companies(Accounts) Rules,2014
and the relevant provisions of the Companies Act 2013 ('the Act'). The accounting policies adopted in the preparation of the financial statements are consistent with those followed in the previous year.
The company is normally viewed as a going concern, that is, as continuing in operation for the foreseeable future. lt is assumed that the enterprise has neither the intention nor the necessity of
liquidation or of curtailing materially the scale of the operations. The restated financial information are presented in Indian National Rupee (INR) & all the amounts included in the restated financial
information have been rounded off to the nearest lakhs, as required by General instructions for preparation of Financial Statements in Division I of Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013, except
number of shares, face value of shares, earning per shares, or wherever otherwise stated. Accounting policies not specifically referred to otherwise are consistent and in consonance with generally
accepted accounting principles in India. All assets and liabilities have been classified as current or non-current as per the Company’s normal operating cycle and other criteria set out in Schedule III to
the Companies Act, 2013. Based on the nature of products and the time between the acquisition of assets for processing and their realization in cash and cash equivalents, the Company has determined
its operating cycle as twelve months for the purpose of current – non-current classification of assets and liabilities. The restated financial information has been prepared by the management to comply
in all material respects with the requirements of:
a) Section 26 of Part I of Chapter III of the Act, 2013;
b) The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018, as amended ("ICDR Regulations"); and
c) The Guidance Note on Reports in Company Prospectuses (Revised 2019) issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), as amended (the “Guidance Note”).




Basis of consolidation:
The consolidated financial statements of the Group includes the financial statements of the parent company, its wholly owned subsidiary, and its joint ventures.
The wholly owned subsidiary is consolidated using the line‑by‑line consolidation method, whereby 100% of its assets, liabilities, income, and expenses are consolidated, as the Group exercises full
control over the subsidiary.
The Group’s interest in joint ventures is consolidated using the proportionate consolidation method. Under this method, the Group includes its share of the joint ventures’ assets, liabilities, income, and
expenses on a line‑by‑line basis in the consolidated financial statements.
All intra‑group balances and transactions between the Group, its subsidiary, and its joint ventures, including unrealized profits or losses arising from such transactions are eliminated to the extent of the
Group’s interest.


These financial statements are prepared by applying uniform accounting policies across the Group and its joint ventures.

Use of estimates:
The preparation and presentation of Financial Statements in conformity with the Indian GAAP, requires the management to make judgements, estimates and assumptions that affect the reported
amounts of revenues, expenses, assets and liabilities and the disclosure of contingent liabilities, at the end of reporting period. Although these estimates are based on management's best knowledge of
current events and actions, uncertainty about these assumptions and estimates could result in outcomes requiring a material adjustment to the carrying amounts of assets or liabilities in future periods.



Going Concern:
The company is normally viewed as a going concern, that is, as continuing in operation for the foreseeable future. lt is assumed that the enterprise has neither the intention nor the necessity of
liquidation or of curtailing materially the scale of the operations.


Revenue recognition:
a) Sale of Goods
Revenue from sale of goods is recognized when the Company has transferred to the buyer the property in the goods for a price or all significant risks and rewards of ownership have been transferred to
the buyer and the Company retains no effective control of the goods transferred to a degree usually associated with ownership; and no significant uncertainty exists regarding the amount of the
consideration that will be derived from the sale of the goods.


b) Sale of services:
Revenue from service transactions is usually recognised as the service is performed by the proportionate completion method. The revenue recognised under this method would be determined on the
basis of contract value, associated costs, number of acts or other suitable basis. For practical purposes, when services are provided by an indeterminate number of acts over a specific period of time,
revenue is recognised on a straight line basis over the specific period. Such performance should be regarded as being achieved when no significant uncertainty exists regarding the amount of the
consideration that will be derived from rendering the service.




                                                                                                  F - 10
(i) Deferred revenue - Deferred revenue represents amounts received or invoiced in advance from the customers. These amounts are recorded as a contract liability until the corresponding services are
rendered. The Company assesses its performance obligations under each contract to determine the appropriate timing of revenue recognition. Revenue is subsequently recognized when the billed
services is transferred to the customer, which may occur over time or at a point in time, depending on the nature of the arrangement.


c) Other Income
Revenue arising from the use by others of enterprise resources yielding interest, royalties and dividends should only be recognised when no significant uncertainty as to measurability or collectability
exists. These revenues are recognised on the following bases:
(i) Interest : on a time proportion basis taking into account the amount outstanding and the rate applicable.

Property Plant and Equipment including Intangible assets:
Property Plant and Equipment's are stated at cost, less accumulated depreciation. Cost includes cost of acquisition including material cost, freight, installation cost, duties and taxes, and other incidental
expenses, incurred up to the installation stage, related to such acquisition. Intangible assets that are acquired by the Company are measured initially at cost. After initial recognition, an intangible asset is
carried at its cost less any accumulated amortisation and any accumulated impairment loss.


Depreciation & Amortisation:
The Company has applied the estimated useful lives as specified in Schedule II of the Companies Act 2013 and calculated the depreciation as per the Written Down Value (WDV) method.
Depreciation on new assets acquired during the year is provided at the rates applicable from the date of acquisition to the end of the financial year. In respect of the assets sold during the year,
depreciation is provided from the beginning of the year till the date of its disposal.


Useful life of Property, Plant and Equipment's

Category                        Useful life
Plant And Machinery             15 years
Furniture and Fittings          10 Years

Electrical Equipment            10 Years


Impairment of assets:
The Management periodically assesses using, external and internal sources, whether there is an indication that an asset may be impaired. An impairment loss is recognised wherever the carrying value
of an asset exceeds its recoverable amount. The recoverable amount is higher of the asset's net selling price and value in use, which means the present value of future cash flows expected to arise from
the continuing use of the asset and its eventual disposal. Reversal of impairment loss is recognised immediately as income in the profit and loss account.

Investments
Investments, which are readily realizable and intended to be held for not more than one year from the date on which such investments are made, are classified as current investments. All other
investments are classified as long-term investments.

Foreign currency transactions:
As the Company did not undertake any foreign currency transactions during the year, the provisions relating to initial recognition, measurement, and treatment of foreign exchange differences under the
applicable accounting standards have not been invoked.

Borrowing Costs

Borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition or construction of qualifying assets are capitalised as part of the cost of such assets. A qualifying asset is one that necessarily takes
substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use. Interest income earned on the temporary investment of specific borrowings pending their expenditure on qualifying assets is deducted from
the borrowing costs eligible for capitalisation. All other borrowing costs are charged to the Statement of Profit and Loss for the period for which they are incurred.


Inventories:
Inventories includes raw material, finished goods, stores & spares, consumables are valued at lower of cost and net realizable value. Materials in transit is valued at cost incurred till date.


      Raw Material and Components - Cost include cost of purchases and other costs incurred in bringing the inventories to their present location and condition. Cost is determined using FIFO
      methodology
      Finished/Semi-Finished Goods - cost includes cost of direct material, labour, other direct cost (Including variable costs) and a proportion of fixed manufacturing overheads allocated based on
      the normal operating capacity but excluding borrowing costs. Cost is determined on weighted average cost basis.
      Net realisable value is the estimated selling price in the ordinary course of business less the estimated cost of completion and the estimated costs necessary to make the sale.
      Adequate allowance is made for obsolete and slow-moving items.

Segment reporting:
The segment reporting is not applicable as per AS 17

Cash and Cash Equivalents:
Cash and cash equivalents comprise cash on hand and Cheque in hand, balance with bank, demand deposits with banks and other short term highly liquid investments that are readily convertible to
known amounts of cash & which are subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value where it has a short maturity of three months or less from the date of acquisition.

Employee Benefits:

A.      Short - term employee benefits:
Leave encashment:
The leave encashment liability upon retirement would not arise as the accumulated leave is reimbursed every year and accounted at actual.


B.       Post-Employment benefits:
Defined benefit plan:
Gratuity liability is a defined benefit obligation and is unfunded. The Company accounts for liability for future gratuity benefits based on the actuarial valuation using Projected Unit Credit Method
carried out as at the end of each financial year.
Defined contribution Plan:
Provident Fund: Eligible employees receive benefit from provident fund covered under the Provident Fund Act. Both the employee and the company make monthly contributions. The employer
contribution is charged off to Profit & Loss Account as an expense.




                                                                                                    F - 11
Taxes on Income:
Income Tax expense is accounted for in accordance with AS-22 "Accounting for Taxes on Income" for both Current Tax and Deferred Tax stated below:

A.        Current Tax:
              Provision for current tax is made in accordance with the provisions of the Income Tax Act, 1961.

B.        Deferred Tax:
              Deferred tax is recognised, subject to the consideration of prudence, as the tax effect of timing difference between the taxable income and accounting income computed for the current
              accounting year using the tax rates and tax laws that have been enacted or substantially enacted by the balance sheet date.
               Deferred tax assets are recognised and carried forward to the extent that there is a reasonable certainty, except arising from unabsorbed depreciation and carried forward losses, that
               sufficient future taxable income will be available against which such deferred tax assets can be realised.


Provisions and Contingent Liabilities:

A provision is recognised if, as a result of past event, the Company has a present legal obligation that can be estimated reliably and it is probable that an outflow of economic benefit will be required to
settle the obligation. Provisions are determined by the best estimate of outflow of economic benefits required to settle the obligation at the reporting date. Where no reliable estimate can be made, a
disclosure is made as contingent liability. A disclosure for a contingent liability is also made when there is a possible obligation or a present obligation that may, but probably will not, require an
outflow of resources. Where there is possible obligation or present obligation in respect of which the likelihood of outflow of resources is remote, no provision or disclosure is made.


Earnings Per Share:
Basic Earnings per share is computed by dividing the net profit after tax by the weighted average number of equity shares outstanding during the period. Diluted earnings per share is computed by
dividing the net profit after tax by the weighted average number of shares considered for deriving basic earnings per share and also the weighted average number of equity shares that could have been
issued upon conversion of all dilutive potential equity shares. The diluted potential equity shares are adjusted for the proceeds receivable had the shares been actually issued at fair value which is the
average market value of the outstanding shares. Dilutive potential equity shares are deemed converted as at the beginning of the period, unless issued at a later date. Dilutive potential equity shares are
determined independently for each period presented.


Cash Flow Statement:
Cash flows are reported using indirect method, whereby net profit/loss before tax is adjusted for the effects of transactions of a non-cash nature, any deferrals or accruals of past or future operating cash
receipts or payments and item of income or expenses associated with investing or financing cash flows. The cash flows from operating, investing and financing activities of the Company are
segregated.
The Company’s cash and cash equivalents consist of cash on hand and in banks and demand deposits with banks, which can be withdrawn at any time, without prior notice or penalty on the principal.
For the purposes of the statement of cash flows, cash and cash equivalents include cash on hand, in banks and demand deposits with banks, net of outstanding bank overdrafts that are repayable on
demand and are considered part of the Company’s cash management system. In the balance sheet, bank overdrafts are presented under borrowings within current liabilities.

          Gratuity - The Present value of obligation is determined based on actuarial valuation using the Projected Unit Credit Method. This method considers each period of service as giving rise to an

          Interest cost: It is the increase in the Plan liability over the accounting period resulting from the operation of the actuarial assumption of the interest rate.

          Actuarial Gain or Loss: occurs when the experience of the Plan differs from that anticipated from the actuarial assumptions. It could also occur due to changes made in the actuarial
          assumptions.

shares outstanding is increased without an increase in reserves. The number of equity shares outstanding before the event is adjusted for the proportionate change in the number of equity shares
outstanding as if the event had occurred at the beginning of the earliest period reported.

Notes:
1. Basis EPS (₹) = Basic earnings per share are calculated by dividing the net restated profit or loss for the year attributable to equity shareholders by the weighted average number of Equity Shares
   outstanding during the year.
2. Diluted EPS (₹) = Diluted earnings per share are calculated by dividing the net restated profit or loss for the year attributable to equity shareholders by the weighted average number of Equity Shares
   outstanding during the year as adjusted for the effects of all dilutive potential Equity Shares during the year.
3. Basis EPS (₹) = Basic earnings per share are calculated by dividing the net restated profit or loss for the year attributable to equity shareholders by the weighted average number of Equity Shares
   outstanding during the year after considering the retrospective effect of bonus shares. The number of equity shares outstanding before the event is adjusted for the proportionate change in the number
   of equity shares outstanding as if the event had occurred at the beginning of the earliest period reported.
4. Diluted EPS (₹) = Diluted earnings per share are calculated by dividing the net restated profit or loss for the year attributable to equity shareholders by the weighted average number of Equity
   Shares outstanding during the year as adjusted for the effects of all dilutive potential Equity Shares during the year. The number of equity shares outstanding before the event is adjusted for the
   proportionate change in the number of equity shares outstanding as if the event had occurred at the beginning of the earliest period reported
5. Calculated as profit for the period/year divided by net worth.
6. Net asset value per equity share means total equity divided by total number of equity shares at year end
7. Net asset value per equity share means total equity divided by weighted average number of equity shares. The number of equity shares outstanding before the event is adjusted for the proportionate
   change in the number of equity shares outstanding as if the event had occurred at the beginning of the earliest period reported
8. EBITDA is calculated as restated profit or loss for the year plus total tax expense, plus depreciation and amortization expense, plus finance costs and minus other income.

Overview

We are an Engineering, Procurement, Construction and Commissioning (“EPCC”) company engaged in providing
integrated infrastructure solutions across multiple domains, with a primary focus on the railway infrastructure, power
transmission & distribution, and water & wastewater treatment sectors. Our expertise spans the entire project lifecycle
design, engineering, procurement, erection, testing, commissioning, and operation & maintenance (“O&M”). We also
operate an in-house manufacturing facility for High-Tension (“HT”) and Low-Tension (“LT”) electrical panels and
compact substations, enabling us to offer customized, reliable, and cost-efficient products that complement our EPCC
activities. We also undertake sub-contracting assignments, providing on-ground execution support for a wide range of
engineering projects.

India’s EPC industry delivers services including design and engineering, procurement, civil works, installation,
commissioning and operation and maintenance covering Railway EPC, Drinking Water & Wastewater Treatment, Power
Distribution Panels and Compact Substation, Transmission and Distribution and SCADA and Automation. India’s
Railway EPC market grew from INR 16.2 thousand crore in FY 20 to INR 30.4 thousand crore in FY 25 and is expected
to reach INR 50.5 thousand crore by FY 30F. The drinking water and wastewater market is projected to reach INR 169.6
thousand crore by FY 30F, supported by growth across panels, transmission and distribution and SCADA segments.
Indian Infrastructure EPC Market is defined as the total domestic revenue generated from engineering, procurement, and
construction (EPC) activities undertaken within India across Railway Infrastructure and Water Infrastructure segments,
along with the related markets for HT/LT Power Distribution Panels, Compact Substations (CSS), and SCADA &
Automation Systems. (Source: Ken Report)

We operate through five interlinked business segments, each contributing to our integrated infrastructure and engineering
solutions framework. Incorporated with the vision of delivering technically robust and cost-effective engineering
solutions, we offer end-to-end project execution capabilities covering design, engineering, procurement, project
management, construction, installation, testing and commissioning.

Our diversified business verticals include:

(a) Railway Electrification & Infrastructure:

Railway Electrification (RE) – We undertake RE and allied infrastructure works represent one of our principal business
segments. We undertake EPCC projects involving the design, supply, erection, testing and commissioning of 25 kV AC
Overhead Electrification (“OHE”) systems, Traction Sub-stations (“TSS”), and Sectioning and Paralleling Posts
(“SP/SSP”). Our scope also includes associated civil works such as foundations, trenches, control room buildings, and

                                                           289
ancillary structures, as well as signalling and telecommunication interface works. We execute projects for zonal railways,
public sector undertakings, and large infrastructure contractors. The Company’s technical proficiency and adherence to
RDSO standards enable efficient, safe, and reliable electrification execution.

Railway Infrastructure Works – Our company does composite nature of work involving civil, electrical, and mechanical
works as part of the Railway Station Redevelopment with allied works and modernization programs initiated by Indian
Railways under the “Amrit Bharat Station Scheme” and other national initiatives. Our services in this domain cover
structural rehabilitation, construction of passenger amenities, illumination systems, internal and external electrification,
foot over bridges, water supply and drainage systems, digital LED signages and integration of automation for energy
management. Through these works, we contribute to the modernization of passenger interface infrastructure and
enhancement of service standards across the Indian Railways network.

Indian Infrastructure EPC Market is defined as the total domestic revenue generated from engineering, procurement, and
construction (EPC) activities undertaken within India across Railway Infrastructure and Water Infrastructure segments,
along with the related markets for HT/LT Power Distribution Panels, Compact Substations (CSS), and SCADA &
Automation Systems. (Source: Ken Report)

The Railway EPC Market is defined as the domestic revenue generated from EPC contracting activities related to railway
electrification, signaling & telecommunication, and civil works in India. Between FY 20 and FY 25, the Railway EPC
market increased from INR 16.2 thousand crore to INR 30.4 thousand crore, at a CAGR of 13.4%. From FY 25 to FY
30F, the market is expected to grow to INR 50.5 thousand crore, at a CAGR of 10.7%. (Source: Ken Report)

In FY 25, India’s Railway EPC market on segmentation by work type, composite infrastructure works, accounted for
51.0%, followed by Electrification of Railway Lines at 13.8%, S&T Works at 12.8%, PEB for Sheds, Warehouses &
Depots at 9.9%, OHE at 5.6%, Traction Substations at 4.3% and Power Transmission & Distribution Networks at 2.6%.
Opportunities for EPC players lie in the execution of electrification, signaling, and station redevelopment works under
flagship programs such as PM Gati Shakti, Amrit Bharat Station Scheme, and Mission Electrification. In addition, high-
speed rail corridors, dedicated freight lines, and multimodal logistics hubs are creating sustained EPC demand across civil
and electrical packages. (Source: Ken Report)

The India Metro Systems EPC Market is defined as the domestic revenue generated from EPC contracting activities
related exclusively to urban metro rail systems in India. India’s metro EPC market has grown steadily from ₹15,000 crore
in FY 19 to an estimated ₹23,500 crore in FY 25, reflecting a CAGR of 7.8%, and is projected to reach ₹34,700 crore by
FY 30F, reflecting an 8.1% CAGR (FY 25 – FY 30F). (Source: Ken Report)

(b) Extra High Tension (“EHT”) Transmission and Distribution Systems:

Our company undertakes turnkey projects in Extra High Tension Transmission and Distribution Systems, covering voltage
levels up to 220 kV. Its scope includes sub-station construction, installation of power transformers, switchgear, control
and relay panels, busbar systems, and distribution networks. We also execute transmission line projects, including
foundation works, tower erection, conductor stringing, and OPGW (“Optical Ground Wire”) integration. Our work in
this vertical supports utilities, public sector undertakings, and industrial clients in strengthening grid reliability and power
distribution efficiency. Its participation aligns with national programs such as the “Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme
(RDSS) and Green Energy Corridors”, emphasizing grid modernization and renewable integration.

The Transmission and Distribution (T&D) Market is defined as the domestic EPC revenue generated from the design,
supply, construction, and commissioning of transmission lines, substations, and distribution networks across India. As of
FY 25, India’s transmission and distribution market size stood at INR 36,000.0 crore, growing at a strong CAGR of 16.2
% over FY 20 – FY 25. The market is projected to reach INR 60,063.0 crore by FY 30F, at a CAGR of 10.8 % (FY 25 –
FY 30F). (Source: Ken Report)

In FY 25, India’s Transmission and Distribution Market Segmentation (INR ‘000 crore) by End User, state segment
accounted for 66.1%, followed by Central segment at 21.9% and Private segment at 11.9%.Opportunities for EPC players
lie in grid expansion, substation construction, feeder modernization driven by government programs such as the Revamped
Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS), Green Energy Corridor, and National Electricity Plan, large-scale push for renewable
evacuation and interregional transmission corridors and growing need for reliable power transmission to support water,
industrial, and renewable infrastructure. (Source: Ken Report)

(c) Water and Wastewater Treatment EPCC:

We provide turnkey EPCC solutions for Water Treatment Plants (“WTP”), Sewage Treatment Plants (“STP”), and
Effluent Treatment Plants (“ETP”), along with associated civil, mechanical, and electrical works. Its capabilities cover

                                                              290
intake wells, pumping stations, rising mains, pipelines, and process automation systems. With ensuring compliance with
CPCB and SPCB norms, we execute projects based on STP technologies such as:

•   MBBR (Moving Bed Biofilm Reactor)
•   SBR (Sequencing Batch Reactor)

These works align with government programs like “Jal Jeevan Mission”, “AMRUT”, and “Namami Gange”, supporting
national goals of water conservation, reuse, and sustainable urban development.

The Drinking Water and Waste Water Treatment Market is defined as the domestic EPC revenue generated from the
design, supply, and execution of drinking water treatment plants, wastewater/sewage treatment plants, distribution
networks, pumping stations, and electro-mechanical works in India. India’s drinking water and wastewater treatment
market expanded from INR 60.5 thousand crore in FY 20 to INR 99.9 thousand crore in FY 25, at a CAGR of 10.6%. It
is expected to reach INR 169.6 thousand crore by FY 30F at a CAGR of ~11.2% (FY 25 – FY 30F). (Source: Ken Report)

In FY 25, India’s Drinking Water and Waste Water Treatment on segmentation by plant type, sewage and water piping
accounted for 33.0%, followed by drinking water treatment plants at 28.0%, effluent treatment plants at 18.5%, sewage
treatment plants at 15.5% and associated infrastructure (including pump houses, reservoirs, pipelines, and control rooms)
at 5.0%.(Source: Ken Report)

Opportunities for EPC players lie in the design and execution of drinking water, sewage, and effluent treatment plants
under flagship government programs such as Jal Jeevan Mission, AMRUT 2.0, and Namami Gange. Rising urbanization,
industrial compliance norms, and Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) requirements are accelerating investments in STPs, ETPs,
and reuse systems. (Source: Ken Report)

(d) Automation and SCADA Systems:

Automation and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (“SCADA”) solutions form an integral part of our service
offerings. We design and implement Programmable Logic Controller (PLC)-based automation systems, RTU and HMI
integration, instrumentation, control panels, and communication networks for remote monitoring and control of
infrastructure assets. Our automation services are applied across its core business sectors railway electrification, water
systems, and power distribution enhancing system reliability, efficiency, and operational safety.

The SCADA & Automation Systems Market is defined as the domestic revenue generated from the design, supply,
execution, and commissioning of SCADA and automation systems across electrical networks, water and wastewater
infrastructure, power projects, and railway installations in India. The Indian SCADA and Automation Systems market has
grown from INR 5.1 thousand crore in FY 20 to INR 7.7 thousand crore in FY 25, reflecting a CAGR of 8.6%. The market
projected to reach INR 12.0 thousand crore by FY 30F, registering a CAGR of 9.3% between FY 25 – FY 30F. (Source:
Ken Report)

In FY 25, India’s SCADA and Automation Systems Market Segmentation by Application, Power Distribution SCADA
accounted for 24.7%, followed by Oil & Gas SCADA at 23.4%, Other Applications SCADA at 16.9%, Manufacturing
SCADA at 15.6%, Water Supply SCADA at 10.4% and Waste Water SCADA at 9.1%.(Source: Ken Report)

The market offers growing opportunities for EPC players in deployment and integration of SCADA systems across power,
water, and industrial assets. With utilities adopting IoT, cloud, and AI-based analytics, EPCs with automation capabilities
can capture value in grid modernization, renewable integration, and smart water networks, supported by government-led
digitalization programs driving steady automation-linked EPC demand. (Source: Ken Report)

(e) Composite supply of HT/LT Distribution Panels along with related services:

We manufacture a wide range of High Tension (HT) and Low Tension (LT) distribution and control panels, including
VCB panels, PCC, MCC, APFC, synchronization panels, and PLC-based automation panels. All panels are designed and
fabricated in accordance with IS/IEC standards, ensuring safety, reliability, and consistent performance. Our in-house
capability supports complete vertical integration from design and fabrication to assembly and testing allowing us to
maintain strict quality control, optimize costs, and ensure timely delivery. In addition to meeting internal project
requirements, this division also contributes to external revenue by supplying panels to third-party clients across industrial
and infrastructure sectors. These panels are typically provided as a composite supply along with our installation, testing
and commissioning services as part of our integrated project execution.




                                                            291
A major strength of this division is our capability to produce Compact Substations (CSS) with capacities up to 2.5 MVA
and voltage levels up to 11 kV. These factory-built, fully integrated substations combine a transformer, HT panel, LT
panel, and protection systems within a single compact enclosure. Their modular design, enhanced safety features, and
reduced installation footprint make them ideal for industrial, commercial, and utility applications. This product segment
represents a key differentiator for us, offering clients faster deployment, improved reliability, and lower lifecycle costs.

We began our operations as a partnership firm in 2014 and were converted into a private limited company in 2022 under
the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013. Headquartered in Mysore, Karnataka, we started as an EPC contractor and
gradually expanded into a diversified infrastructure and utility solutions provider with integrated capabilities across
design, engineering, installation, testing, commissioning, and O&M. Over the years, we have built relationships with
government organizations, PSUs, utilities, and private enterprises across India. Our structure allows us to leverage
synergies between our EPC and manufacturing divisions, enabling us to deliver end-to-end, technology-driven, and cost-
optimized infrastructure solutions across sectors.

Our business is supported by a Board of Directors with diverse functional and sectoral experience, providing strategic
direction and oversight to the Company’s operations. The Board comprises Agrahara Chamaraje Gowda Abhinandan,
Promoter and Managing Director, with over eleven years of experience in EPC, railway infrastructure,
SCADA/automation, transmission and distribution and utility projects; Mahadevappa Tejus, Promoter and Whole-time
Director, with over nine years of experience in project execution, procurement and construction management; and
Hosahalli Appagigowda Savitha, Promoter, Chairman and Executive Director, with over seven years of experience in
administration, governance and operational management. The Board also includes Anala, Promoter and Non-Executive
Director, with engineering and industry experience in human resources and organizational development; Kikkeri Putte
Gowda Jayaramu, Independent Director, with over thirty-four years of experience in urban infrastructure, water supply
and sanitation projects; and Mysore Govindaraju Yashwanthkumar, Independent Director, with over nine years of
experience in finance, accounting and taxation. The collective expertise of the Board supports informed decision-making,
effective oversight of operations, and adherence to governance and compliance requirements.

Our strength lies in integrated engineering capability, experienced technical team, and proven execution across complex,
time-bound projects. Our business model focuses on project management, vendor partnerships, in-house design expertise,
and commitment to quality, safety, and sustainability. We have long-term relationships with public sector undertakings,
state utilities, and private clients, including participation in infrastructure programs led by Indian Railways and other
government agencies. With a presence across multiple sectors and a growing order book, we combine EPC experience
with in-house manufacturing through a vertically integrated model that supports cost efficiency, design flexibility, and
quality control. This enables execution of multidisciplinary projects in power, water, and industrial automation within
defined timelines. Our vision is to enhance execution and profitability in small and medium EPC contracts while adopting
emerging technologies to deliver sustainable infrastructure under Public-Private Partnership (“PPP”) models.

Significant factors affecting our Financial Condition and Results of Operations

Our financial condition and results of operations are influenced by several factors, including infrastructure sector growth,
our ability to secure and execute Engineering, Procurement, Construction and Commissioning contracts, cost management
including raw material procurement, working capital requirements arising from project-based operations, and the
performance of our manufacturing operations for electrical panels and substations. The following factors have
significantly affected, and are expected to continue to affect, our financial condition and results of operations.

Growth in Infrastructure Development in Railway Electrification, Power Transmission & Distribution and Water
Infrastructure Sectors

Our business is closely linked to infrastructure development in sectors such as railway electrification, power transmission
and distribution, and water and wastewater treatment systems. Demand for our EPCC services depends largely on
infrastructure investments undertaken by the Government of India, state governments, public sector undertakings
(“PSUs”), and infrastructure developers. Government initiatives such as railway electrification programs, strengthening
of transmission networks, renewable energy integration, and expansion of water supply and wastewater treatment
infrastructure have supported the growth of infrastructure projects across India. These initiatives have increased the
demand for EPC contractors capable of delivering integrated engineering and construction solutions. Our revenue from
operations increased from ₹1,311.95 lakhs in Fiscal 2023 to ₹3,345.13 lakhs in Fiscal 2024 and ₹3,415.68 lakhs in Fiscal
2025, primarily driven by the execution of infrastructure projects across these sectors. However, our financial performance
remains dependent on the pace of infrastructure investments and project awards. Any slowdown in government capital
expenditure, delays in infrastructure project approvals, or changes in public procurement policies may adversely affect
the demand for our services and impact our revenues.

Dependence on Government Entities and Public Sector Clients for Infrastructure Projects

A significant portion of infrastructure projects in India are undertaken by government departments, public sector
undertakings, and government-backed authorities. As a result, EPCC contractors such as us often derive a substantial
portion of their revenues from projects awarded by such entities. Projects undertaken for government clients typically
involve detailed tendering processes, technical qualification requirements, and compliance with regulatory and contractual
obligations. While such projects offer opportunities for large-scale infrastructure development, they may also involve
extended approval processes, complex documentation requirements, and longer payment cycles. Our financial
performance is therefore influenced by the pace of tendering activities, the availability of government-funded
infrastructure projects, and the timely execution and payment of such contracts. Any reduction in government
infrastructure spending, delays in project awards, or changes in procurement frameworks may affect the availability of
new projects and impact our revenue growth.

Ability to Secure New EPCC Contracts and Maintain a Healthy Order Book

Our revenue generation depends significantly on our ability to secure new EPCC contracts and subcontracting assignments
through competitive bidding processes. Infrastructure projects are generally awarded based on evaluation criteria such as
technical capabilities, past project experience, financial capacity, execution capabilities, and pricing competitiveness.

As of September 30, 2025, contract value of our consolidated order book stood at approximately ₹15,615.23 lakhs, which
provides visibility of revenue for future financial periods. Our order book to revenue ratio for Fiscal 2025 was
approximately 4.86x, reflecting the level of project pipeline available for execution. The value and timing of new project
awards directly affect our revenue growth and operational performance. Increased competition from other EPC contractors
may lead to pricing pressures and reduced project margins. Our ability to maintain strong technical capabilities, efficient
project execution systems, and relationships with infrastructure authorities will continue to be important in securing new
contracts and sustaining our order pipeline.

Project Execution Efficiency, Raw Material Procurement and Dependence on Subcontractors and Vendors



                                                                                                294
Our financial performance is significantly influenced by our ability to execute EPCC projects efficiently and manage
project costs effectively. EPCC projects involve engineering design, procurement of materials and equipment,
construction and erection activities, testing and commissioning, and in certain cases operation and maintenance services.
The cost structure of our projects includes procurement of materials and equipment such as electrical components, cables,
switchgear, copper, aluminium, steel structures, transformers and other engineering equipment. Fluctuations in raw
material prices may impact project costs and profitability, particularly in fixed-price contracts.

We also rely on subcontractors and vendors for certain project execution activities, including specialized engineering
works, civil construction, installation works, and supply of project equipment. The availability, reliability, and
performance of subcontractors and suppliers play an important role in the timely execution of projects.

Delays or performance issues involving subcontractors, supply chain disruptions, or increases in material costs may result
in project delays, cost overruns, or reduced margins. Our ability to effectively manage subcontractor performance,
procurement planning, and project scheduling is therefore important for maintaining operational efficiency and
profitability. Our EBITDA was ₹153.58 lakhs in Fiscal 2023, ₹507.03 lakhs in Fiscal 2024, and ₹682.38 lakhs in Fiscal
2025, with EBITDA margins of 11.71%, 15.16% and 19.98% respectively.

Working Capital Requirements and Integration of Electrical Panel Manufacturing with our EPCC Operations

Our EPCC operations require significant working capital due to the project-based nature of our contracts. Infrastructure
projects typically involve milestone-based billing structures, where payments are linked to project progress and
certification of completed work. As a result, our working capital is deployed in trade receivables, inventories of project
materials and equipment, advances to suppliers, and other project execution expenses. As of March 31, 2025, our trade
receivables amounted to ₹3,619.02 lakhs, representing approximately 106% of our revenue for Fiscal 2025, with a
receivable cycle of approximately 238 days. In addition to our EPCC activities, we operate an in-house manufacturing
facility for High-Tension (“HT”) and Low-Tension (“LT”) electrical panels and compact substations. These products are
used in power distribution systems for infrastructure projects and complement our EPCC operations by enabling
customized equipment supply and improved project execution timelines. The integration of manufacturing with our EPC
operations allows us to maintain quality control, optimize procurement timelines, and reduce dependence on third-party
suppliers for certain electrical equipment. However, the performance of this segment may be affected by fluctuations in
raw material prices, production efficiencies, and demand for electrical panels from infrastructure projects. Efficient
management of project cash flows, receivables, and manufacturing operations is therefore critical to maintaining our
liquidity position and financial performance.

Competition

We operate in a highly competitive environment in the infrastructure and engineering procurement, construction and
commissioning (“EPCC”) industry in India. The infrastructure contracting sector is highly fragmented and includes
several domestic EPC contractors, engineering companies and specialized infrastructure service providers. Our success
depends on our ability to effectively compete for projects through competitive bidding processes and to differentiate our
capabilities through efficient project execution, technical expertise, cost competitiveness and timely completion of
projects.

To remain competitive, we must continue to maintain our execution capabilities, deliver projects within stipulated
timelines, and comply with the quality and technical standards required by our clients. In addition, we must continuously
focus on improving our operational efficiencies, optimizing procurement and project execution costs, and effectively
managing resources across our projects. Our ability to successfully bid for and execute projects also depends on
maintaining our reputation with clients, demonstrating strong project execution capabilities, and maintaining compliance
with contractual and regulatory requirements.

Many of our competitors may be larger than us and may benefit from greater financial resources, broader project
portfolios, established industry relationships and economies of scale. Such competitors may have the ability to bid more
aggressively for projects, which could increase pricing pressure in competitive tenders. If we are unable to compete
effectively in securing new projects or maintaining our competitive position in the infrastructure sector, it may adversely
affect our order book, revenues, and financial performance.

Further, the competitive nature of the EPCC industry may result in reduced project margins as contractors compete on
pricing to secure infrastructure contracts. Any sustained pressure on project pricing or inability to control project execution
costs may materially adversely affect our profitability, financial condition and results of operations.

   expenses, assets and liabilities and the disclosure of contingent liabilities, at the end of reporting period. Although
   these estimates are based on management's best knowledge of current events and actions, uncertainty about these
   assumptions and estimates could result in outcomes requiring a material adjustment to the carrying amounts of assets
   or liabilities in future periods.

   The restated financial information has been prepared and presented under historical cost convention on the accrual
   basis of accounting in accordance with the Generally Accepted Accounting Principles in India (“GAAP”) and comply
   with the mandatory Accounting Standards (“AS”) specified under section 133 of the Companies Act 2013, read with
   Rule 7 of the Companies(Accounts) Rules,2014 and the relevant provisions of the Companies Act 2013 ('the Act').
   The accounting policies adopted in the preparation of the financial statements are consistent with those followed in
   the previous year. The company is normally viewed as a going concern, that is, as continuing in operation for the
   foreseeable future. lt is assumed that the enterprise has neither the intention nor the necessity of liquidation or of
   curtailing materially the scale of the operations. The restated financial information are presented in Indian National
   Rupee (INR) & all the amounts included in the restated financial information have been rounded off to the nearest
   lakhs, as required by General instructions for preparation of Financial Statements in Division I of Schedule III of the

   Accounting policies not specifically referred to otherwise are consistent and in consonance with generally accepted
   accounting principles in India. All assets and liabilities have been classified as current or non-current as per the
   Company’s normal operating cycle and other criteria set out in Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013. Based on the

   balance, the Company has determined its operating cycle as twelve months for the purpose of current – non-current
   classification of assets and liabilities. The restated financial information has been prepared by the management to

b) Segment Information



                                                           296
   There is no reportable segment identified as per Accounting Standard 17 on the basis of which segment information
   is required to be disclosed.

c) Basis of consolidation

   The consolidated financial statements of the Group include the financial statements of the parent company, its wholly
   owned subsidiary, and its joint ventures.

   The wholly owned subsidiary is consolidated using the line‑by‑line consolidation method, whereby 100% of its assets,
   liabilities, income, and expenses are consolidated, as the Group exercises full control over the subsidiary.

   The Group’s interest in joint ventures is consolidated using the proportionate consolidation method. Under this
   method, the Group includes its share of the joint ventures’ assets, liabilities, income, and expenses on a line‑by‑line
   basis in the consolidated financial statements.

   All intra‑group balances and transactions between the Group, its subsidiary, and its joint ventures, including unrealized
   profits or losses arising from such transactions are eliminated to the extent of the Group’s interest.

d) Use of estimates

   The preparation and presentation of Financial Statements in conformity with the Indian GAAP, requires the
   management to make judgements, estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of revenues, expenses,
   assets and liabilities and the disclosure of contingent liabilities, at the end of reporting period. Although these estimates
   are based on management's best knowledge of current events and actions, uncertainty about these assumptions and
   estimates could result in outcomes requiring a material adjustment to the carrying amounts of assets or liabilities in
   future periods.

e) Going Concern

   The company is normally viewed as a going concern, that is, as continuing in operation for the foreseeable future. lt
   is assumed that the enterprise has neither the intention nor the necessity of liquidation or of curtailing materially the
   scale of the operations.

f) Revenue recognition

    i)   Sale of goods - Revenue from sale of goods is recognized when the Company has transferred to the buyer the
         property in the goods for a price or all significant risks and rewards of ownership have been transferred to the
         buyer and the Company retains no effective control of the goods transferred to a degree usually associated with
         ownership; and no significant uncertainty exists regarding the amount of the consideration that will be derived
         from the sale of the goods.

    ii) Sale of service - Revenue from service transactions is usually recognised as the service is performed by the
        proportionate completion method. The revenue recognised under this method would be determined on the basis
        of contract value, associated costs, number of acts or other suitable basis. For practical purposes, when services
        are provided by an indeterminate number of acts over a specific period of time, revenue is recognised on a
        straight-line basis over the specific period. Such performance should be regarded as being achieved when no
        significant uncertainty exists regarding the amount of the consideration that will be derived from rendering the
        service.

    iii) Deferred revenue - Deferred revenue represents amounts received or invoiced in advance from the customers.
         These amounts are recorded as a contract liability until the corresponding services are rendered. The Company
         assesses its performance obligations under each contract to determine the appropriate timing of revenue
         recognition. Revenue is subsequently recognized when the billed services is transferred to the customer, which
         may occur over time or at a point in time, depending on the nature of the arrangement.

    g) Other Income

         Revenue arising from the use by others of enterprise resources yielding interest, royalties and dividends should
         only be recognised when no significant uncertainty as to measurability or collectability exists. Interest has been
         recognised on a time proportion basis taking into account the amount outstanding and the rate applicable.

    h) Property Plant and Equipment including Intangible assets

                                                             297
     Property Plant and Equipment's are stated at cost, less accumulated depreciation. Cost includes cost of acquisition
     including material cost, freight, installation cost, duties and taxes, and other incidental expenses, incurred up to
     the installation stage, related to such acquisition. Intangible assets that are acquired by the Company are measured
     initially at cost. After initial recognition, an intangible asset is carried at its cost less any accumulated
     amortisation and any accumulated impairment loss.

i)   Depreciation & Amortisation

     The Company has applied the estimated useful lives as specified in Schedule II of the Companies Act 2013 and
     calculated the depreciation as per the Written Down Value (WDV) method. Depreciation on new assets acquired
     during the year is provided at the rates applicable from the date of acquisition to the end of the financial year. In
     respect of the assets sold during the year, depreciation is provided from the beginning of the year till the date of
     its disposal.

j)   Useful life of Property, Plant and Equipment's

      Category                                                   Useful life
      Plant And Machinery                                        15 years
      Furniture and Fittings                                     10 Years
      Office Equipment                                           5 Years
      Computer and Equipment                                     3 Years
      Electrical Equipment                                       10 Years

k) Impairment of assets

     The Management periodically assesses using, external and internal sources, whether there is an indication that
     an asset may be impaired. An impairment loss is recognised wherever the carrying value of an asset exceeds its
     recoverable amount. The recoverable amount is higher of the asset's net selling price and value in use, which
     means the present value of future cash flows expected to arise from the continuing use of the asset and its eventual
     disposal. Reversal of impairment loss is recognised immediately as income in the profit and loss account.

l)   Investments

     Investments, which are readily realizable and intended to be held for not more than one year from the date on
     which such investments are made, are classified as current investments. All other investments are classified as
     long-term investments.

m) Foreign currency transactions

     As the Company did not undertake any foreign currency transactions during the year, the provisions relating to
     initial recognition, measurement, and treatment of foreign exchange differences under the applicable accounting
     standards have not been invoked.

n) Borrowing Costs

     Borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition or construction of qualifying assets are capitalised
     as part of the cost of such assets. A qualifying asset is one that necessarily takes substantial period of time to get
     ready for its intended use. Interest income earned on the temporary investment of specific borrowings pending
     their expenditure on qualifying assets is deducted from the borrowing costs eligible for capitalisation. All other
     borrowing costs are charged to the Statement of Profit and Loss for the period for which they are incurred.

o) Inventories

     i) Raw Material and components - cost include cost of purchases and other costs incurred in bringing the
        inventories to their present location and condition. Cost is determined using FIFO methodology.

     ii) Finished/Semi-Finished Goods - cost includes cost of direct material, labour, other direct cost (Including
        variable costs) and a proportion of fixed manufacturing overheads allocated based on the normal operating
        capacity but excluding borrowing costs. Cost is determined on weighted average cost basis.



                                                         298
p) Cash and Cash Equivalents

     Cash and cash equivalents comprise cash on hand and Cheque in hand, balance with bank, demand deposits with
     banks and other short term highly liquid investments that are readily convertible to known amounts of cash &
     which are subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value where it has a short maturity of three months or less
     from the date of acquisition.

q) Employee Benefits

     i)   Short term employee benefits –

     (1) Leave encashment - The leave encashment liability upon retirement would not arise as the accumulated
         leave is reimbursed every year and accounted at actual.

     ii) Long term employee benefits –

          (1) Defined benefit plan - Gratuity liability is a defined benefit obligation and is unfunded. The Company
              accounts for liability for future gratuity benefits based on the actuarial valuation using Projected Unit
              Credit Method carried out as at the end of each financial year.

          (2) Defined contribution plan - Provident Fund: Eligible employees receive benefit from provident fund
              covered under the Provident Fund Act. Both the employee and the company make monthly
              contributions. The employer contribution is charged off to Profit & Loss Account as an expense.

r)   Taxes on Income

     Income Tax expense is accounted for in accordance with AS-22 "Accounting for Taxes on Income" for both
     Current Tax and Deferred Tax stated below:

     i) Current Tax – Provision for current tax is made in accordance with the provisions of the Income Tax Act,
     1961.

     ii) Deferred Tax - Deferred tax is recognised, subject to the consideration of prudence, as the tax effect of timing
     difference between the taxable income and accounting income computed for the current accounting year using
     the tax rates and tax laws that have been enacted or substantially enacted by the balance sheet date. Deferred tax
     assets are recognised and carried forward to the extent that there is a reasonable certainty, except arising from
     unabsorbed depreciation and carried forward losses, that sufficient future taxable income will be available against
     which such deferred tax assets can be realised.

s)   Provisions and contingent liabilities

     A provision is recognised if, as a result of past event, the Company has a present legal obligation that can be
     estimated reliably and it is probable that an outflow of economic benefit will be required to settle the obligation.
     Provisions are determined by the best estimate of outflow of economic benefits required to settle the obligation
     at the reporting date. Where no reliable estimate can be made, a disclosure is made as contingent liability. A
     disclosure for a contingent liability is also made when there is a possible obligation or a present obligation that
     may, but probably will not, require an outflow of resources. Where there is possible obligation or present
     obligation in respect of which the likelihood of outflow of resources is remote, no provision or disclosure is
     made.

t)   Earnings per share

     Basic Earnings per share is computed by dividing the net profit after tax by the weighted average number of
     equity shares outstanding during the period. Diluted earnings per share is computed by dividing the net profit
     after tax by the weighted average number of shares considered for deriving basic earnings per share and also the
     weighted average number of equity shares that could have been issued upon conversion of all dilutive potential
     equity shares. The diluted potential equity shares are adjusted for the proceeds receivable had the shares been
     actually issued at fair value which is the average market value of the outstanding shares. Dilutive potential equity
     shares are deemed converted as at the beginning of the period, unless issued at a later date. Dilutive potential
     equity shares are determined independently for each period presented.

u) Cash flow statement

                                                        299
              Cash flows are reported using indirect method, whereby net profit/loss before tax is adjusted for the effects of
              transactions of a non-cash nature, any deferrals or accruals of past or future operating cash receipts or payments
              and item of income or expenses associated with investing or financing cash flows. The cash flows from operating,
              investing and financing activities of the Company are segregated.

              The Company’s cash and bank balances consist of cash on hand and in banks and demand deposits with banks,
              which can be withdrawn at any time, without prior notice or penalty on the principal. For the purposes of the
              statement of cash flows, cash and bank balance include cash on hand, in banks and demand deposits with banks,
              net of outstanding bank overdrafts that are repayable on demand and are considered part of the Company’s cash
              management system. In the balance sheet, bank overdrafts are presented under borrowings within current
              liabilities.

Segment Information

There is no reportable segment identified on the basis of which segment information is required to be disclosed.

Period ended September 30, 2025

Long term borrowings

Long-term borrowings stood at ₹546.92 lakhs, comprising secured term loans from banks of ₹102.39 lakhs and unsecured
borrowings aggregating ₹444.53 lakhs, including loans from NBFCs of ₹170.04 lakhs and loans and advances from related
parties of ₹274.49 lakhs. These borrowings have been utilized for capital expenditure, working capital and general
corporate purposes.

Short term borrowings

Short-term borrowings stood at ₹1,660.19 lakhs, of which bank overdrafts accounted for ₹1,576.48 lakhs. The overdraft
balance with Bank of Baroda stood at ₹526.06 lakhs, representing an increase of ₹209.29 lakhs as compared to March
2025. The outstanding balance under the State Bank of India LC facility stood at ₹1,050.42 lakhs.

Trade Payables

35.23% of the total trade payables, amounting to ₹376.37 lakhs, pertained to MSME vendors, while the balance of ₹691.88
lakhs related to non-MSME vendors. Further, 92.75% of the total trade payables fall within the ageing bracket of less than
one year.

Interest payables to vendor under MSME Act, 2006 has been accrued amounting to ₹5.80 lakhs as at September 2025.

Inventories

As at September 30, 2025, total inventory, comprising primarily work-in-progress, stood at ₹1,790.57 lakhs. The increased
inventory was primarily attributable to the higher level of ongoing project execution during the period, particularly in
relation to EPC contracts undertaken for railway infrastructure, power transmission and distribution projects, and water
and wastewater treatment systems. As projects typically involve longer execution cycles, a portion of the materials
procured, and work performed remains classified as work-in-progress until the corresponding project milestones are
completed and revenue is recognized.

Trade Receivables

Out of the total receivables, 64.20% are outstanding for less than 6 months, while 33.82% fall within the 6 months to 1
year category. A much smaller portion relates to older balances, with 1.04% outstanding for 1–2 years, 0.71% for 2–3
years, and only 0.23% remaining unpaid for more than 3 years. The increase in balance from March 2025 is primarily
attributable to higher sales volumes during the fiscal year and extended credit cycle offered to select clients in line with
our strategy to strengthen long-term customer relationships. The rise also reflects an increase in outstanding dues from
both new and existing clients.

Allowance for doubtful debts has been provided for at ₹58.99 lakhs.

As at September 30, 2025, total commitments amounted to ₹627.16 lakhs on a consolidated basis. The entire balance
represents other commitments in the form of bank guarantees.

Key Components of Income and Expenses

We report our income and expenditure in the following manner:

Total Income

Our total income comprises of revenue from operations and other income.

Revenue from operations: consists primarily of income from EPC services to Indian Railways, water and wastewater
treatment technology projects, Extra High Voltage (220KV/110KV/66KV/27KV/11KV) transmission and distribution
work projects and composite supply of HT/LT Distribution Panels along with related services. Product revenue is
generated by Core4 Energy Ltd (subsidiary company) from the in-house manufacturing and supply of High and Low
Tension (HT/LT) electrical distribution panels, control and relay panels, PLC and SCADA panels, and other custom-built
electrical manufacturing. These vertical supports both internal EPC requirements and third-party industrial and
infrastructure clients.

Other income: includes interest earned on deposits, discounts received, balances written off and other ancillary incomes.

Total Expenses

Our total expenses comprise of cost of materials consumed, other direct expenses, changes in inventories of work-in-
progress, employee benefits expenses, finance costs, depreciation and amortization expenses, and other expenses.

Cost of Material Consumed: primarily represents the cost of raw materials purchased for the Company’s operations during
the relevant periods.

Other Direct expenses: includes subcontract charges, material consumed, labour charges, rent, travelling and conveyance,
office expenses, service charges, site expenses, freight and forwarding charges.

Changes in Inventories of Work-in-Progress: represents the net increase or decrease in work-in-progress at the beginning
of the year and end of the year.

Employee benefits expenses: comprises of salaries & wages, directors’ remuneration, contribution to provident fund,
gratuity expenses and staff welfare expenses.

Finance costs: consists of interest expenses on loans, borrowings, and other borrowing costs.

                                                          303
Depreciation and Amortization Expenses: includes depreciation on tangible and intangible assets.

Other Expenses: majorly comprise of bad debt, bank charges, miscellaneous expenses, office maintenance, rates & taxes,
legal and professional fees, renting of machineries, travelling expenses, warranty expenses, etc.

Period ended September 30, 2025

Total Income

Our total income for the period ended September 30, 2025 was ₹4,730.74 lakhs based on Restated Consolidated Financial
Information. This income was primarily driven by our revenue from operations, which continued to reflect our revenue
from four major streams of revenue. For further details, please see “- Period ended September 30, 2025 - Revenue from
operations” and “- Period ended September 30, 2025 – Other Income” below.

Revenue from operations: Revenue from operations of ₹4,706.97 lakhs was primarily driven by four revenue streams:
Railway Electrification & Infrastructure, Extra High Tension (“EHT”) Transmission and Distribution Systems, Water and
Wastewater Treatment EPCC and Automation and SCADA Systems. Revenue from the aforesaid services (Engineering,
Procurement and Construction contracts) amounted to ₹4,699.32 lakhs, while revenue of ₹7.65 lakhs from the sale of
products represents panel sales generated by our subsidiary and consolidated in our books.

                                                          304
Other Income: comprising interest income, amounted to ₹23.76 lakhs for the period ended September 30, 2025.

Total Expenses

Cost of Material Consumed: primarily represents the cost of raw materials and project-related materials procured for our
operations, including inputs required for the manufacturing of HT and LT electrical panels and compact substations as
well as materials utilised in the execution of our EPCC projects across railway infrastructure, power transmission and
distribution, and water and wastewater treatment sectors. For the period ended September 30, 2025, the cost of materials
consumed stood at ₹2,816.45 lakhs.

Other Direct expenses: Other direct expenses for the period ended September 30, 2025 stood at ₹876.86 lakhs. The
expenses during the period primarily comprised labour charges of ₹453.97 lakhs, rent of ₹154.26 lakhs, freight and
forwarding charges of ₹74.46 lakhs, site expenses of ₹75.82 lakhs, transport charges of ₹42.66 lakhs, travelling and
conveyance expenses of ₹33.72 lakhs, and service charges of ₹27.34 lakhs. Material consumed under this head stood at
₹14.63 lakhs during the period. The level of other direct expenses during the period reflects ongoing project execution
activities and operational requirements during the period.

Changes in Inventories of Work-in-Progress: Changes in inventories of work-in-progress resulted in an income of ₹349.59
lakhs for the period ended September 30, 2025. The movement reflects the difference between opening WIP of ₹1,440.98
lakhs and closing WIP of ₹1,790.57 lakhs during the period. The change primarily reflects variations in project execution
progress and the timing of recognition of work-in-progress during the period.

Employee benefit expense: Employee benefit expenses amounted to ₹296.62 lakhs, comprising salaries and wages of
₹255.38 lakhs, contributions to PF of ₹22.94 lakhs, gratuity expenses of ₹5.63 lakhs, directors’ remuneration of ₹7.05
lakhs, and staff welfare expenses of ₹5.61 lakhs.

Finance cost: Finance costs amounted to ₹95.08 lakhs, comprising interest expenses of ₹91.23 lakhs and other borrowing
costs of ₹3.85 lakhs.

Depreciation and Amortization: Depreciation amounted to ₹2.57 lakhs driven by depreciation on tangible assets.

Other expenses: Other expenses amounting to ₹181.31 lakhs are primarily driven by rates and taxes of ₹84.64 lakhs, legal
and professional fees of ₹19.59 lakhs, miscellaneous expenses of ₹13.92 lakhs, research and development expenses of
₹9.74 lakhs, bank charges of ₹8.97 lakhs and the remaining balance attributable to other incremental expenses.

Tax expenses

Our total tax expense stood at ₹206.00 lakhs for the period ended September 30, 2025. This comprised: Current tax
expenses of ₹209.31 lakhs; Deferred tax credits of ₹3.30lakhs. The deferred tax credits primarily arose on account of
timing differences in the treatment of depreciation on fixed assets and recognition of employee benefit obligations under
accounting standards vis-à-vis tax records.
